idiom: bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh

idiom: cut off

idiom: saw his father's nakedness

idiom: I have raised my hand to the LORD God Most High

idiom: go to your fathers in peace

idiom: go to my maidservant

idiom: a wild donkey of a man

idiom: Walk before Me

idiom: cut off from his people
meaning: In this verse, to be destroyed or wiped out, as all living things were killed by the flood.

idiom: had not gone near her
meaning: He had not had sexual relations with her.

idiom: possess the gates of their enemies

idiom: Place your hand under my thigh

idiom: was gathered to his people
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: making me a stench
meaning: You have made me hated by the people of the land, which leaves us exposed to their revenge.

idiom: I will go down to Sheol mourning for my son
meaning: You will cause my death in old age through grief; I would spend the rest of my life in sorrow until I go to the grave.

idiom: raise up offspring for your brother
meaning: To give a dead man an heir by marrying his widow. Her child would count as his son, so his family line and land stayed attached to his name.

idiom: make sport of us
meaning: To take shameless, indecent liberties with, and wantonly insult, the women of the household.

idiom: make sport of me
meaning: To take shameless, indecent liberties with, and wantonly insult, the women of the household.

idiom: Pharaoh will lift up your head

idiom: he lifted up the heads
meaning: Here it means Pharaoh called the two prisoners out and took up their cases to decide their fate. It works as a wordplay: one was raised back to his post, the other raised up to be hanged.

idiom: As surely as Pharaoh lives

idiom: account for his blood
meaning: To be held guilty and punished for someone's death, as God demands payment for shed blood.

idiom: you will bring my gray hair down to Sheol in sorrow
meaning: You will cause my death in old age through grief; I would spend the rest of my life in sorrow until I go to the grave.

idiom: bear the guilt before you
meaning: To be held responsible for a sin and so face its punishment.

idiom: brought the gray hair of your servant our father down to Sheol in sorrow
meaning: You will cause my death in old age through grief; I would spend the rest of my life in sorrow until I go to the grave.

idiom: I will bear the guilt before you
meaning: To be held responsible for a sin and so face its punishment.

idiom: made me a father to Pharaoh
meaning: "Father" was a title for a king's chief minister; Joseph became Pharaoh's most trusted adviser, with a father's authority and care.

idiom: Joseph's own hands will close your eyes
meaning: Closing a dead person's eyes was the last loving duty of the closest relative. The promise meant Jacob would die in peace with Joseph alive and at his side.

idiom: when I lie down with my fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: The scepter will not depart from Judah

idiom: Issachar is a strong donkey

idiom: Naphtali is a doe set free

idiom: I am about to be gathered to my people
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: he was gathered to his people
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: brought up on Joseph's knees
meaning: The children were born while Joseph was alive and were received by him. Some take this as Joseph, the family head, formally adopting or acknowledging them as his own. Others say it only means he held them on his lap and loved them.

idiom: you have made us a stench before Pharaoh
meaning: You have wrecked our good name with Pharaoh and his officials and made them loathe us; like being "in bad odour" with someone, but stronger.

idiom: you have placed in their hand a sword to kill us
meaning: A proverbial complaint that Moses and Aaron had given Pharaoh and his men a pretext and opportunity to destroy the Israelites, exposing them to deadly danger.

idiom: the hand of the LORD
meaning: God's own power acting directly, with no human go-between; here it strikes Egypt's livestock with a deadly plague as a judgment.

idiom: not even a dog will snarl at man or beast
meaning: A proverb for complete safety and calm: Israel would meet no harm and not even the slightest hostile sound, not so much as a dog growling at them, while Egypt was struck.

idiom: cut off from Israel
meaning: The offender would be expelled from the community of Israel and lose its privileges, with God himself threatening to step in and root him out.

idiom: cut off from the congregation of Israel
meaning: Anyone who ate leavened bread during the feast, native or foreigner, faced removal or destruction from the community of Israel.

idiom: a sign for you on your hand and a reminder on your forehead
meaning: Something kept always in view and in mind, as if it were tied on the hand or worn on the forehead. It keeps the rescue from Egypt and God's commands constantly remembered. Later Jews took it literally and wore small scrolls in boxes (tefillin, or phylacteries).

idiom: a sign on your hand and a symbol on your forehead

idiom: Your right hand, O LORD
meaning: A human-like picture of God's might: his right hand stands for his overwhelming power, shown in crushing Israel's enemies.

idiom: You stretched out Your right hand
meaning: God put forth his power; one move of his hand was enough to destroy his enemies at once.

idiom: a hand was lifted up toward the throne of the LORD
meaning: Either a solemn oath, made with a hand raised toward God's throne in heaven, that war on Amalek would never end; or a charge that Amalek had raised its hand against God's throne by attacking God's people. Some scholars change the word to "banner" instead.

idiom: Do not draw near to a woman
meaning: Do not have sexual relations, even with your own wife, so as to stay ritually pure for a solemn holy event.

idiom: the LORD will break out against them
meaning: If they cross the boundary, God will suddenly strike them with deadly judgment.

idiom: He will break out against them
meaning: If they cross the boundary, God will suddenly strike them with deadly judgment.

idiom: visiting the iniquity of the fathers on their children
meaning: God lets the punishment and consequences of parents' sin, especially idolatry, fall on their descendants for several generations. Examples include disease, poverty, and bad example. This applies above all to children who keep on hating God and follow their fathers' ways.

idiom: take the name of the LORD your God in vain
meaning: To misuse God's name for something empty or false. Some sources say it mainly forbids swearing a false oath in God's name; others say it also covers careless, frivolous, or insincere use, such as casual oaths, cursing, or magic.

idiom: within your gates
meaning: Living in your towns and settlements. "Gates" stands for the cities, so the phrase means the foreigner who has settled among the Israelites in their land.

idiom: eye for eye, tooth for tooth
meaning: The law that the penalty must match the injury, no more and no less. It was a rule for judges and courts, not a license for personal revenge, and was often settled by a matching payment rather than literal maiming.

idiom: twists the words of the righteous
meaning: A bribe corrupts justice. It skews the ruling of a judge who would otherwise be fair, or it overturns the case of the innocent party, so the person who is in the right loses.

idiom: I will fulfill the number of your days
meaning: To let people live out their full natural lifespan with no early death, as a sign of God's blessing.

idiom: bear the iniquity
meaning: The high priest, through his consecrated office, took on himself the guilt and flaws attached to the people's sacred offerings and removed them, so that God would accept the gifts.

idiom: cut off from among his people
meaning: A Sabbath-breaker put himself outside God's covenant and was treated as an outlaw, expelled from the people. Some take it as another way of saying execution, or as a death sent by God when the crime was secret.

idiom: a stiff-necked people
meaning: Stubborn and rebellious. The picture is a work animal that stiffens its neck and refuses to be steered by its driver or to accept the yoke.

idiom: He will visit the iniquity of the fathers on their children

idiom: they prostitute themselves to their gods

idiom: shall bear his iniquity
meaning: He stays guilty and must face the penalty for his offense.

idiom: a man lies with a woman

idiom: a man lies with her

idiom: cut him off from among his people
meaning: God himself would turn his anger on anyone who ate blood and remove that person from the community, usually by death, especially when the offense was hidden from human judges.

meaning: Anyone who ate blood would be put to death.

meaning: He stays guilty and must face the penalty for his offense.

meaning: God would remove the offender from his people by death. Some take this to mean that the people's stoning of him is God's own way of cutting him off; others take it to mean that God himself would strike him down if the crime went unpunished for lack of evidence.

idiom: I will set My face against that man

meaning: To look the other way on purpose: to wink at or tolerate the crime and not accuse or punish the offender, whether from indifference or from quiet approval.

idiom: prostituting themselves with Molech
meaning: To worship other gods or idols. Israel was seen as bound to God like a wife to a husband, so idolatry was treated as unfaithfulness in marriage. The phrase also fits the sexually impure rites that went with some pagan worship.

meaning: God turns toward someone with a fixed, hostile resolve. It means he is determined to oppose them in anger and bring punishment on them.

idiom: uncovered the nakedness of his sister
meaning: Having sexual relations with his own sister.

idiom: cut off from among their people
meaning: Both offenders would be removed from the community. Some see a formal public expulsion, while others take it as death by the authorities or by God, or as dying without children.

idiom: uncovered the source of her blood
meaning: Having sexual relations with a woman during her menstrual period. Saying that both the man and the woman "uncovered" the flow shows that both knew her condition and freely agreed to the act, so both shared the guilt.

idiom: both shall bear their iniquity
meaning: He stays guilty and must face the penalty for his offense.

idiom: uncovered the nakedness of his uncle
meaning: Sleeping with his uncle's wife, which counted as dishonoring the uncle, since her nakedness belonged to him; the kinship was too close.

idiom: uncovered the nakedness of his brother
meaning: Having sexual relations with (marrying) a brother's wife, which counted as dishonoring the brother himself, since her nakedness belonged to him.

idiom: cut off from My presence

idiom: cut off your supply of bread
meaning: God would send famine and take away bread, the staple that keeps people alive, so that food would be scarce, strictly rationed and never enough.

idiom: walk in fury against you

meaning: For God to turn His face toward someone and look at them with special care and favor.

idiom: put My name on the Israelites
meaning: The priests spoke God's sacred name over the people as they blessed them. This marked Israel as God's own people, and God promised to make the blessing real.

meaning: God asks whether his reach and strength are too limited to do what he promised. It is a rebuke to doubt: his power has no limit, and his word will come true.

idiom: The land we explored devours its inhabitants
meaning: The spies' bad report that Canaan was a land where people did not survive. idiom: they will be like bread for us
meaning: The enemy would be as easy to consume as food, so Israel would swallow them up and defeat them easily; some add that the enemy's goods would end up feeding Israel.

idiom: as one man
meaning: All together at one time, in a single sudden blow, as one person might be struck down.

idiom: visit the iniquity of the fathers upon their children
meaning: God lets the punishment and consequences of parents' sin, especially idolatry, fall on their descendants for several generations. Examples include disease, poverty, and bad example. This applies above all to children who keep on hating God and follow their fathers' ways.

idiom: at the cost of their own lives
meaning: Men whose sin forfeited their lives, bringing death on themselves.

idiom: bear the iniquity involving the sanctuary
meaning: The priests and Levites were answerable for any offense against or defilement of the holy place, whether done by themselves or by the people. They would suffer the penalty for it, and through their office they would also deal with that guilt and remove it.

idiom: bear the iniquity involving your priesthood
meaning: The priests alone were accountable for faults in carrying out their priestly duties, both their own mistakes and those they allowed in others, and they had to atone for the sin attached to their official acts.

idiom: your father's house
meaning: The wider ancestral family or clan descended from one forefather; here it means Aaron's larger kin group (the Levites, or the Kohathite branch), as distinct from his own sons the priests.

idiom: a permanent covenant of salt

idiom: I am your portion and your inheritance
meaning: The priests got no land of their own. Instead the LORD himself was their possession and provider: they lived on what was given to him and belonged especially to him, which was worth more than any land.

idiom: bear their iniquity
meaning: The Levites were held responsible for guarding the sanctuary. They would carry the guilt and penalty for failures or neglect in that duty, including any wrongful approach by the people that they allowed.

idiom: Aaron will be gathered to his people

idiom: he lifted up an oracle

idiom: Water will flow from his buckets

idiom: all flesh

meaning: If anyone attacks, harms or kills someone.

meaning: The guilt and responsibility for a person's death rests on that person (or on whoever is named), not on anyone else. Someone who dies through his own neglect or choice has only himself to blame.

idiom: his blood will be on our heads
meaning: The guilt and responsibility for a person's death rests on that person (or on whoever is named), not on anyone else. Someone who dies through his own neglect or choice has only himself to blame.

idiom: the hand of the LORD is mighty
meaning: God's power is great beyond limit and can do what nature cannot, shown by drying up the Jordan for Israel to cross.

idiom: their hearts melted and their spirits failed
meaning: People lost all courage and hope from fear, as if their hearts had turned to water, leaving them no strength to act or resist.

idiom: rolled away the reproach of Egypt
meaning: God removed a disgrace that had clung to Israel since Egypt, marked by their circumcision and their arrival in the promised land. Sources disagree about what the disgrace was: Egyptian taunts that God had led them out only to die in the desert, the shame of having been slaves, or their uncircumcised state.

idiom: for going out, and for coming in
meaning: Caleb is still fit for active life: to go out to war and return, and to carry out public duties.

idiom: from the hand of the LORD
meaning: In this verse, being delivered out of the hand of the LORD means being spared the punishing judgment that would otherwise have fallen on the whole people.

idiom: going the way of all the earth
meaning: To be about to die, taking the road every human must take sooner or later.

idiom: incline your hearts
meaning: To turn the heart toward the LORD fully and willingly, loving, fearing, and serving him alone. This means giving up any hidden attachment to other gods, including idols of the heart.

idiom: gathered to their fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: the hand of the LORD was against them
meaning: God's power was working against Israel, so every battle or undertaking they began ended in defeat and disaster, as the punishment He had warned of.

idiom: prostituted themselves with other gods
meaning: To worship other gods or idols. Israel was seen as bound to God like a wife to a husband, so idolatry was treated as unfaithfulness in marriage. The phrase also fits the sexually impure rites that went with some pagan worship.

idiom: your hands will be strengthened
meaning: To encourage, support and enable people in their work; here the king's goodwill let them carry on and finish rebuilding the temple.

idiom: Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your possession
meaning: A mocking, cowardly question: "Have you already captured and beaten these kings?" Until victory was certain, they would not risk the kings' revenge by helping Gideon.

idiom: prostituted themselves with the Baals
meaning: To worship other gods or idols. Israel was seen as bound to God like a wife to a husband, so idolatry was treated as unfaithfulness in marriage. The phrase also fits the sexually impure rites that went with some pagan worship.

idiom: If you had not plowed with my heifer
meaning: Using another man's heifer to plow meant getting results through someone else. Samson is saying they did not solve the riddle by their own wits but by working on his wife to get the secret. The sources reject the view that it hints at adultery.

idiom: Refresh your heart with a morsel of bread
meaning: To eat a meal and renew one's strength and spirits. Here the host urges his guest to eat before setting off on the journey.

idiom: refresh your heart
meaning: To eat a meal and renew one's strength and spirits. Here the host urges his guest to eat before setting off on the journey.

idiom: from Dan to Beersheba
meaning: The whole land of Israel, from its northern edge (Dan) to its southern edge (Beersheba). In other words, all Israel.

idiom: the hand of the LORD has gone out against me
meaning: God Himself had acted against Naomi and afflicted her, taking her husband and sons and leaving her poor and alone.

idiom: Spread the corner of your garment over me
meaning: A request for marriage and protection: a man covering a woman with the edge of his cloak was a sign that he took her as his wife and under his care. Here Ruth asks this of Boaz as her kinsman-redeemer.

idiom: raise up the name of the deceased
meaning: To give a dead man an heir by marrying his widow. Her child would count as his son, so his family line and land stayed attached to his name.

idiom: his name will not disappear from among his brothers or from the gate of his home
meaning: To give a dead man an heir by marrying his widow. Her child would count as his son, so his family line and land stayed attached to his name.

idiom: may your house become like the house of Perez
meaning: A blessing wishing the couple a large and honored family line, like that of Perez, Judah's son, whose descendants were very numerous and from whom the Bethlehem clan came.

idiom: the LORD remembered her
meaning: God paid attention to Hannah, answered her prayer and let her become pregnant.

idiom: my horn is exalted in the LORD
meaning: The horn, as on a strong wild ox, stands for strength and power. Raising someone's horn means giving them strength, victory and honor over their enemies.

idiom: He will exalt the horn of His anointed
meaning: The horn, as on a strong wild ox, stands for strength and power. Raising someone's horn means giving them strength, victory and honor over their enemies.

idiom: kick at My sacrifice
meaning: Pictures an overfed, pampered animal that kicks at the owner who feeds it. It means treating God's offerings with contempt, abusing them out of greed and pride.

idiom: I will cut off your strength
meaning: God would break the power and standing of Eli and his family line, so that its members would die young and none would reach old age.

idiom: I will cause your eyes to fail
meaning: Eyes that fail are eyes worn out by weeping. Some of Eli's line would survive only to see their family ruined and to waste away in grief over it.

idiom: I will build for him an enduring house
meaning: God would give the faithful priest a secure, lasting family line of descendants, and for some commentators that includes keeping the priestly office in his family. Commentators disagree over who the priest is (Zadok or Samuel), but not over what the phrase means.

idiom: the ears of all who hear it will tingle
meaning: The news will be so shocking and terrible that anyone who hears it will be stunned, as if both ears had been struck.

idiom: He let none of Samuel's words fall to the ground
meaning: God made every word Samuel spoke as a prophet come true, so none failed. This proved he was a true prophet.

idiom: each man fled to his tent
meaning: The army was completely beaten and broke up, and every survivor ran off to his own home instead of regrouping. "Tent" is a leftover word from Israel's nomadic past, meaning home.

idiom: the hand of the LORD was heavy on the people of Ashdod
meaning: God's power came down hard on them as punishment, striking them with painful, deadly disease and ruin.

idiom: His hand is heavy upon us
meaning: God's afflicting hand presses hard on the sufferer, so his pain is greater than even his groaning shows. Some read the Hebrew in Job 23:2 as Job's own hand weighing on or holding back his groans, and the verse's wording is unclear.

idiom: the hand of the LORD was against the Philistines
meaning: God's power kept opposing the Philistines, so their attacks on Israel were held back and defeated for as long as Samuel led.

idiom: all your father's house
meaning: The wider ancestral family or clan descended from one forefather; here it means Aaron's larger kin group (the Levites, or the Kohathite branch), as distinct from his own sons the priests.

idiom: they came out together as one man
meaning: The people turned out in complete unity and all at once, as if by common agreement, the whole nation rising together in response to the summons.

idiom: here is the king walking before you
meaning: The king now leads and rules the nation in every area of life, not only in war; the picture is of a shepherd walking in front of his flock.

idiom: I have walked before you
meaning: Samuel had led and governed the people openly as their prophet and judge since his youth, so they could testify to how he had behaved in office.

idiom: you have not found anything in my hand
meaning: You found nothing wrong in my conduct; I took no bribe and did no injustice, so my record as your leader is clean.

idiom: the hand of the LORD will be against you
meaning: God would turn His power against the people and punish them with judgments such as war, famine, or captivity, and having a king would not shield them.

idiom: Israel has become a stench to the Philistines
meaning: Israel had become hated by the Philistines, who were provoked and angered against them.

idiom: a man after His own heart
meaning: A man God chose who fits what God wants, someone who would carry out God's will (David, in contrast to Saul).

idiom: his eyes brightened
meaning: He was refreshed and got his strength back. The dimness and faintness of hunger and exhaustion left him, and this showed in his eyes becoming clear and lively again.

idiom: my eyes have brightened
meaning: He was refreshed and got his strength back. The dimness and faintness of hunger and exhaustion left him, and this showed in his eyes becoming clear and lively again.

idiom: his father's house
meaning: The wider ancestral family or clan descended from one forefather; here it means Aaron's larger kin group (the Levites, or the Kohathite branch), as distinct from his own sons the priests.

idiom: Let no man's heart fail
meaning: Let no one lose courage or become discouraged.

idiom: sin against innocent blood
meaning: To bring blood-guilt on yourself by killing a person who has done nothing to deserve death.

idiom: do not ever cut off your loving devotion from my household
meaning: Jonathan asks David never to stop keeping his covenant loyalty and kindness to Jonathan's family and descendants, even after David has become all-powerful and his enemies are gone.

idiom: the house of David
meaning: David's family and descendants, which is why Jonathan's covenant reached past David himself to his line after him.

idiom: You son of a perverse and rebellious woman
meaning: A harsh insult meaning "you stubborn, rebellious wretch"; in that culture slurring a man's mother was the deepest insult to the man himself, and the words aim at the son, not the mother.

idiom: feigned madness in their hands
meaning: David pretended to be insane in front of the Philistines, while he was in their power, so they would see him as harmless and let him go.

idiom: strengthened his hand in God
meaning: To encourage, support and enable people in their work; here the king's goodwill let them carry on and finish rebuilding the temple.

idiom: A dead dog? A flea?
meaning: An expression of utter contempt: the person is vile, worthless and despicable.

idiom: wipe out my name from my father's house
meaning: The wider ancestral family or clan descended from one forefather; here it means Aaron's larger kin group (the Levites, or the Kohathite branch), as distinct from his own sons the priests.

idiom: you will not cut off my descendants
meaning: In this verse, to be destroyed or wiped out, as all living things were killed by the flood.

idiom: bound securely by the LORD your God in the bundle of the living
meaning: God will keep your life safe under His own care, the way valuables were tied up in a bag to protect them. Later Jewish tradition also applied it to life after death.

idiom: he became like a stone
meaning: Nabal collapsed and lay stiff and senseless, likely a stroke or faint, from the shock of the news (fear, rage or wounded pride), and never recovered.

idiom: What evil is in my hand?
meaning: A protest of innocence: what crime have I committed? David indirectly declares he is guiltless and challenges Saul to name a reason for hunting him.

idiom: do not let my blood fall to the ground
meaning: A plea not to die a violent death. Sources differ on the point: some take it as "do not kill me, for the LORD sees and will avenge my blood"; others as "do not drive me to die in exile, far from the land where the LORD is present and worshiped."

idiom: the king of Israel has come out to look for a flea
meaning: David says he is so insignificant that the king chasing him is a waste of effort and beneath a king's dignity, like hunting a single flea or a lone bird in the hills.

idiom: march in and out with me
meaning: David's conduct and service with Achish in the army, which Achish found trustworthy.

idiom: Your blood be on your own head
meaning: The guilt and responsibility for a person's death rests on that person (or on whoever is named), not on anyone else. Someone who dies through his own neglect or choice has only himself to blame.

idiom: Your glory, O Israel, lies slain on your heights
meaning: Israel's pride and finest ornament, Saul and Jonathan (and the nation's warriors), lie dead on the mountain heights of Gilboa; some instead read "gazelle" as a name for Jonathan alone.

idiom: the bow of Jonathan did not retreat
meaning: Jonathan's arrows never missed; they always struck and killed the enemy. The poetic picture is of weapons that "drink" the blood of the slain, praising him as a deadly, victorious warrior.

idiom: the house of Saul and the house of David
meaning: David's family and descendants, which is why Jonathan's covenant reached past David himself to his line after him.

idiom: Am I the head of a dog
meaning: An angry denial: "Am I something utterly worthless and contemptible, and a traitor siding with Judah?" Dogs were despised scavengers, so "dog" was an insult.

idiom: May it whirl over the head of Joab
meaning: A forceful curse: may the guilt and punishment for Abner's blood come crashing down on Joab and his family, so that his line always suffers disease, weakness, violent death, or poverty.

idiom: led Israel out and brought them back
meaning: David led Israel's troops out to battle and brought them home safely; he was their real leader.

idiom: I have cut off all your enemies from before you
meaning: In this verse, to be destroyed or wiped out, as all living things were killed by the flood.

idiom: He Himself will establish a house for you
meaning: God will give David a lasting family line and keep the kingship in his descendants.

idiom: when your days are fulfilled
meaning: When your lifetime reaches its appointed end and you die. One source says it also implies a full, natural lifespan rather than an early or violent death.

idiom: you rest with your fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: with the rod of men
meaning: God will punish wrongdoing in David's heir with the kind of discipline humans receive, as a father corrects a son, to correct him and not to destroy him or take back his favor.

idiom: a dead dog like me
meaning: An expression of utter contempt: the person is vile, worthless and despicable.

idiom: they would extinguish my one remaining ember
meaning: Killing her only surviving son would put out the last live coal of her household, wiping out her one remaining hope and her husband's name and family line.

idiom: let me see the king's face
meaning: To be allowed into the king's presence, meaning full return to his favor and to court life, not the half-pardon of being kept away.

idiom: this dead dog
meaning: An expression of utter contempt: the person is vile, worthless and despicable.

idiom: the hands of all who are with you will be strengthened
meaning: To encourage, support and enable people in their work; here the king's goodwill let them carry on and finish rebuilding the temple.

idiom: you have become a stench to your father
meaning: You have made yourself hateful to your father, past any chance of making peace. Taking the king's concubines was an unforgivable insult and a claim to the throne, which left Absalom's followers sure there could be no reconciliation.

idiom: we will descend on him like dew on the ground
meaning: A huge army will come down on David suddenly, quietly, and with no way to stop it, covering every spot the way dew covers every blade of grass, so that nobody escapes.

idiom: the forest devoured more people than the sword
meaning: More of the defeated army died while fleeing through the rough, tangled forest, where they were hemmed in and hunted down, than died in the fighting itself.

idiom: Every man to his tent, O Israel!
meaning: A rallying cry to break away: renounce loyalty to David's royal house and go home to look after themselves, leaving David's line to rule only its own tribe.

idiom: a city that is a mother in Israel
meaning: A leading or chief city of a region (a metropolis) with smaller towns and villages under it, which were thought of as its daughters.

idiom: has lifted up his hand against the king
meaning: To rebel against the king, taking hostile, treasonous action and stirring up revolt.

idiom: David sought the face of the LORD
meaning: He earnestly pleaded for God's favor and presence, asking God to look kindly on him rather than turn away.

idiom: the horn of my salvation
meaning: The horn, as on a strong wild ox, stands for strength and power. Raising someone's horn means giving them strength, victory and honor over their enemies.

idiom: The cords of Sheol entangled me
meaning: The speaker was in deadly danger, as if the grave were a hunter that had caught him in its ropes and nets and was about to drag him in.

idiom: at the blast of the breath of His nostrils
meaning: A picture of God's angry snorting, His furious rebuke, felt as a storm wind strong enough to drive back the sea and lay bare the earth's foundations, as at the Red Sea.

idiom: the blood of the men who risked their lives
meaning: Putting their lives in serious danger to do something. David saw the water as costing their lives, so drinking it would be like drinking their blood.

idiom: let us fall into the hand of the LORD
meaning: To choose a punishment that comes straight from God (the plague), trusting His mercy, instead of one carried out through people, such as enemies in war or dealers in a famine.

idiom: let Your hand fall upon me and my father's house
meaning: The wider ancestral family or clan descended from one forefather; here it means Aaron's larger kin group (the Levites, or the Kohathite branch), as distinct from his own sons the priests.

idiom: rests with his fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: go the way of all the earth
meaning: To be about to die, taking the road every human must take sooner or later.

idiom: do not let his gray head go down to Sheol in peace
meaning: Do not let him reach a peaceful natural death in old age unpunished; see that he pays with his life.

idiom: bring his gray head down to Sheol in blood
meaning: Do not spare the old man for his age; see that he dies a violent death by execution for his guilt rather than a natural one.

idiom: David rested with his fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: at the expense of his life
meaning: Adonijah's request would cost him his life; by making it he had brought his own death on himself.

idiom: Their blood will come back upon the heads of Joab
meaning: The guilt and responsibility for a person's death rests on that person (or on whoever is named), not on anyone else. Someone who dies through his own neglect or choice has only himself to blame.

idiom: your blood will be on your own head
meaning: The guilt and responsibility for a person's death rests on that person (or on whoever is named), not on anyone else. Someone who dies through his own neglect or choice has only himself to blame.

idiom: not knowing how to go out or come in
meaning: Solomon confesses he lacks the experience to conduct affairs and govern as king.

idiom: out of the furnace for iron
meaning: Egypt is pictured as an iron-smelting furnace, a place of fierce heat, meaning the harsh bondage and suffering Israel endured there.

idiom: incline our hearts to Himself
meaning: To turn the heart toward the LORD fully and willingly, loving, fearing, and serving him alone. This means giving up any hidden attachment to other gods, including idols of the heart.

idiom: cut off Israel from the land
meaning: God would uproot Israel from the land he gave them and send them into exile and captivity, if they wholly abandoned him.

idiom: will hiss
meaning: Passersby will make a hissing sound in scorn and mockery at the ruined temple, showing contempt for the fallen people.

idiom: David had rested with his fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: Solomon rested with his fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: I will scourge you with scorpions
meaning: The new king threatens to rule far more harshly than his father. Whips stand for a lighter punishment, and "scorpions" for something much more painful, probably a lash fitted with barbs or metal points, or simply a figure of speech for cruel treatment.

idiom: Look now to your own house, O David
meaning: The northern tribes rejecting the rule of David's family: let David's line look after its own tribe, Judah, and stop ruling over them.

idiom: To your tents, O Israel
meaning: A rallying cry to break away: renounce loyalty to David's royal house and go home to look after themselves, leaving David's line to rule only its own tribe.

idiom: as one burns up dung until it is gone
meaning: God will wipe out Jeroboam's family completely and with contempt, clearing away every last trace of it the way people get rid of filthy refuse they find disgusting.

idiom: I will cut off from Jeroboam every male
meaning: In this verse, to be destroyed or wiped out, as all living things were killed by the flood.

meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: before whom I stand
meaning: Whom I serve. It names the speaker as God's servant and minister, standing ready to do His will and speaking with His authority.

idiom: who eat at Jezebel's table
meaning: Kept on the queen's payroll: the prophets were fed and supported out of Jezebel's royal household supplies, a sign of her special favor and her backing of their cult.

idiom: the hand of the LORD came upon Elijah
meaning: God's power came on Elijah, moving and guiding him and giving him more than natural strength, so he could outrun the king's chariot.

idiom: whose mouths have not kissed him
meaning: Who have never worshiped Baal. Idol worshipers showed devotion by kissing the idol's image or blowing a kiss toward it, so not kissing him means refusing that homage.

idiom: if enough dust remains of Samaria for each of my men to have a handful
meaning: This was a boast and a threat at once. Ben-hadad swears he will grind Samaria to rubble, and that his army is so huge the whole heap would not give each soldier even one handful of dust.

idiom: The one putting on his armor should not boast like one taking it off
meaning: A proverb: don't brag about winning before the fight is over. Only the man taking off his armor after the battle has earned the right to boast.

idiom: I will cut off from Ahab every male
meaning: In this verse, to be destroyed or wiped out, as all living things were killed by the flood.

idiom: Every man to his own city, and every man to his own land
meaning: The order to end the campaign and break up the army, with every soldier going home. Here it was given after the king died in battle.

idiom: Ahab rested with his fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: Jehoshaphat rested with his fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: the chariots and horsemen of Israel
meaning: The prophet (Elijah) was Israel's real defense and strength. Through his counsel, prayers and standing with God he protected the nation better than its war chariots and cavalry, which were the chief military power of the time.

idiom: He used to pour water on the hands of Elijah
meaning: He was Elijah's personal servant and constant companion; pouring water for a master to wash his hands was a servant's job.

idiom: What have we to do with each other?
meaning: We have no common ground, and you have no claim on me. It is a sharp refusal that amounts to telling the person to go away.

idiom: the hand of the LORD came upon Elisha
meaning: God's power came on Elisha in the spirit of prophecy, a gift from God and not his own ability, showing him what to say.

idiom: Tie up your garment
meaning: Gather up your long loose robe at the waist so you can move quickly; get ready to go in haste.

idiom: even if the LORD were to make windows in heaven
meaning: A mocking expression of disbelief. Even if God opened floodgates in the sky, as at the Flood, and rained down grain, such sudden plenty still could not happen.

idiom: Jehoram rested with his fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: Tuck your cloak under your belt
meaning: Gather up your long loose robe at the waist so you can move quickly; get ready to go in haste.

idiom: the LORD lifted up this burden against him
meaning: The LORD spoke this prophetic sentence of doom against Ahab. A "burden" here means a solemn prophetic message of judgment.

idiom: Jehu rested with his fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: Jehoahaz rested with his fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: Jehoash rested with his fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: A thistle in Lebanon sent a message to a cedar in Lebanon
meaning: A short fable mocking a proud weakling who claims to be equal to someone far greater (asking for a man's daughter in marriage meant claiming equal rank), only to be casually crushed. It warned Amaziah not to start a fight he could not win.

idiom: King Amaziah rested with his fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: Jeroboam rested with his fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: Jotham rested with his fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: I am your servant and your son
meaning: A formal offer of submission: Ahaz makes himself Assyria's vassal, ready to obey and pay tribute in return for military protection.

idiom: Ahaz rested with his fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: the LORD had torn Israel away from the house of David
meaning: David's family and descendants, which is why Jonathan's covenant reached past David himself to his line after him.

idiom: children have come to the point of birth, but there is no strength to deliver them
meaning: A saying for a desperate crisis: things have reached the deciding moment, but every human resource is gone and there is no strength left to get through it, like a woman in labor too weak to deliver.

idiom: Incline Your ear, O LORD
meaning: To incline the ear is to bend it toward someone and listen closely. It asks for, or trusts in, God's attentive hearing and answering of prayer, even the quiet sighs of the oppressed.

idiom: the Daughter of Jerusalem shakes her head behind you
meaning: Jerusalem mocks the Assyrian king with scornful gestures as he retreats in disgrace, as if to say his defeat was bound to happen.

idiom: The Virgin Daughter of Zion despises you and mocks you
meaning: A poetic name for the people of Jerusalem (Zion), pictured as a woman.

idiom: With the soles of my feet I have dried up all the streams of Egypt
meaning: Sennacherib's boast that nothing can stop his army: just as he digs wells in dry deserts, even Egypt's many river channels will be no barrier when he marches on them, as if they dried up under his feet.

idiom: grass on the rooftops, scorched before it is grown
meaning: Grass that sprouted in the thin soil of flat roofs soon dried up in the sun without ever ripening. It means something short-lived and useless, like enemies who perish before their plans come to anything.

idiom: your going out and coming in
meaning: In this verse, going in and out of the holy place most likely means regularly frequenting the place of worship or seat of judgment, carrying on one's public life; the verse is read in many different ways.

idiom: Hezekiah turned his face to the wall
meaning: He turned away from the people around his couch to be alone with God, hiding his grief and praying in private.

idiom: I have walked before You faithfully
meaning: Live all of life knowing you are always in God's sight: obeying Him, trying to please Him, and relying on Him in everything.

idiom: Hezekiah rested with his fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: I will stretch out over Jerusalem the measuring line used against Samaria and the plumb line used against the house of Ahab
meaning: Builders' tools used for marking out what to tear down are used here as a standard of judgment. God would judge Jerusalem by the same rule he used on Samaria and Ahab's family, and destroy it just as thoroughly.

idiom: Manasseh rested with his fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: I will indeed gather you to your fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: Jehoiakim rested with his fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: Reuben defiled his father's bed
meaning: Reuben had sex with his father Jacob's concubine Bilhah. This shameful sin against his father cost him the rights of the firstborn.

idiom: they prostituted themselves with the gods of the peoples of the land
meaning: To worship other gods or idols. Israel was seen as bound to God like a wife to a husband, so idolatry was treated as unfaithfulness in marriage. The phrase also fits the sexually impure rites that went with some pagan worship.

idiom: The Philistines followed hard after Saul
meaning: The Philistines kept close on Saul's heels and chased him relentlessly, making Saul and his sons their main target.

idiom: at the risk of their lives
meaning: Putting their lives in serious danger to do something. David saw the water as costing their lives, so drinking it would be like drinking their blood.

idiom: How can I drink the blood of these men who risked their lives?
meaning: Putting their lives in serious danger to do something. David saw the water as costing their lives, so drinking it would be like drinking their blood.

idiom: a spear like a weaver's beam
meaning: A detail that likens this giant's weapon to Goliath's, so that Benaiah's fight with him recalls David's combat with Goliath.

idiom: like the army of God
meaning: Adding "of God" was a Hebrew way of saying something is very great; it means a huge, mighty army.

idiom: you go to be with your fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: let me fall into the hand of the LORD
meaning: To give oneself up to punishment sent by God, trusting His mercy, rather than be at the mercy of people, whose anger has no limit.

idiom: as a footstool for our God
meaning: The ark (specifically its lid, the mercy-seat) was pictured as the resting place for God's feet, since God was thought of as enthroned above it between the cherubim; a temple housing the ark was thus a house for God's footstool, heaven being his true throne.

idiom: by His hand upon me
meaning: By God's inspiring influence and revelation, so the temple plan came from God and not from David's own ideas.

idiom: walk before You with all their hearts
meaning: Live all of life knowing you are always in God's sight: obeying Him, trying to please Him, and relying on Him in everything.

idiom: a covenant of salt
meaning: A lasting agreement that cannot be broken. Salt keeps things from spoiling, it went with sacrifices, and sharing salt at a meal sealed friendship and loyalty, so a salt covenant stood for something permanent and binding.

idiom: Abijah rested with his fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: has escaped from your hand
meaning: Because Asa trusted the Syrian king and not God, he lost the chance to defeat Syria's army as well; that victory slipped out of his reach.

idiom: rested with his fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: set his face to seek the LORD
meaning: He firmly made up his mind to seek God's help, earnestly and with full purpose.

idiom: to prostitute themselves
meaning: To worship other gods or idols. Israel was seen as bound to God like a wife to a husband, so idolatry was treated as unfaithfulness in marriage. The phrase also fits the sexually impure rites that went with some pagan worship.

idiom: Uzziah rested with his fathers
meaning: To die and join one's ancestors in death. Calling death sleep makes it gentle and familiar, and it hints that the dead will wake again.

idiom: He will not turn His face away from you
meaning: God turns away and withholds his favor and help, in anger or seeming indifference. He acts as if he takes no notice of his people's suffering and does not step in to rescue them.

idiom: the arm of flesh
meaning: Merely human strength, which is weak and frail, in contrast to God's power; an "arm" means a helper or source of strength.

idiom: all that has been placed in their hands
meaning: Everything that has been entrusted or assigned to them to do.

idiom: the people assembled as one man
meaning: The people gathered with one mind and common purpose, acting together unanimously and promptly, not necessarily meaning every single person came.

idiom: to strengthen their hands
meaning: To encourage, support and enable people in their work; here the king's goodwill let them carry on and finish rebuilding the temple.

idiom: the hand of the LORD his God was upon him
meaning: God's kind favor and care rested on Ezra and guided events for him, moving the king to grant everything he asked.

idiom: which is in your hand
meaning: The law of God that you possess and handle, and in which you are thoroughly skilled and at home.

idiom: the hand of the LORD my God was upon me
meaning: God's favor, guidance and protection were with Ezra, and that gave him the courage and strength to take on the task.

idiom: the holy seed
meaning: The people of Israel, set apart and consecrated to God by his covenant, a people meant to stay separate from other nations.

idiom: to lift up my face to You
meaning: To face God openly; Ezra is too ashamed of the people's guilt to raise his face toward God.

idiom: light to our eyes
meaning: Suffering was pictured as making the eyes dim. Brightened eyes meant renewed strength, life and gladness.

idiom: to give us a stake in His holy place
meaning: A tent peg or nail driven firmly in gave the returned remnant a secure, settled footing at God's sanctuary in Jerusalem, something firm to hold them up.

idiom: strengthen my hands
meaning: To encourage, support and enable people in their work; here the king's goodwill let them carry on and finish rebuilding the temple.

idiom: Their hands will be weakened in the work
meaning: Hands hanging down helplessly: an image of terror and despair, losing all courage and strength to act or fight back.

idiom: they grew fat
meaning: They became well fed and prosperous from the land's plenty, and the luxury made them proud, self-indulgent and forgetful of God (as in "grew fat and kicked").

idiom: Skin for skin!
meaning: A common saying of that time: a person will give up anything to save himself. Satan uses it to claim that Job accepted his losses only because he himself was unharmed, and that he will turn on God once his own body is struck. Commentators disagree on how the saying worked literally, but agree on this point.

idiom: that night did not shut the doors of the womb
meaning: Job blames the night of his beginning for not stopping him from being conceived or born; had it done so, he would never have lived to know his present suffering.

idiom: whom God has hedged in
meaning: Boxed in by God on every side, like a traveler whose road is blocked or a prisoner, with no way out of his suffering and confusion. It reverses the earlier sense of God's protective hedge around Job.

idiom: houses of clay
meaning: Human bodies, which are made from dust and rest on it. They are weak, short-lived and easily destroyed.

idiom: their tent cords pulled up
meaning: Human life is like a tent: when the cord holding it up is pulled out, the tent falls and the person dies, suddenly and without having become truly wise. Some read the word as "excellency" instead of "cord," but they also take it to mean that whatever is best in people disappears at death.

idiom: the sword in their mouth
meaning: The harmful words of powerful enemies, such as slander, lies, threats and false charges, which cut and destroy like a sword. God rescues the helpless from them.

idiom: to unleash His hand and cut me off
meaning: In this verse, to be destroyed or wiped out, as all living things were killed by the flood.

idiom: to swallow my spittle
meaning: A proverb for the shortest moment of time; Job begs for even a brief breathing space of relief.

idiom: we were born yesterday
meaning: We have lived only a short time and so have little experience or understanding compared with the generations before us. That is why one should learn from the wisdom passed down by the ancients.

idiom: strengthen the hand of evildoers
meaning: To encourage, support and enable people in their work; here the king's goodwill let them carry on and finish rebuilding the temple.

idiom: pour me out like milk, and curdle me like cheese
meaning: A poetic picture of God forming a child in the womb. Something liquid at first gradually firms up into a body, the way milk thickens into cheese. Job is saying that God made him.

idiom: I cannot lift my head
meaning: A head hangs down in grief and shame. Lifting it means God raises the person out of despair and humiliation, comforting them and restoring their honor.

idiom: lift up your hands to Him
meaning: Raising or spreading out the hands was the posture of prayer; it means to pray and ask God for help.

idiom: you will lift up your face without blemish
meaning: To face God openly; Ezra is too ashamed of the people's guilt to raise his face toward God.

idiom: the eyes of the wicked will fail
meaning: The wicked will wear themselves out looking for relief or rescue that never comes. Their hopes will come to nothing.

idiom: you are the people with whom wisdom itself will die
meaning: Sarcasm: Job mocks his friends for acting as though they alone hold all the wisdom in the world, so that it will vanish when they die.

idiom: Your maxims are proverbs of ashes; your defenses are defenses of clay
meaning: Your much-quoted wise sayings are as worthless as ashes, and the arguments you hide behind are as weak as clay walls that crumble easily.

idiom: Why do You hide Your face
meaning: God turns away and withholds his favor and help, in anger or seeming indifference. He acts as if he takes no notice of his people's suffering and does not step in to rescue them.

idiom: fill his belly with the hot east wind
meaning: To fill your mind with empty, worthless ideas and then blow them out as loud, violent talk that does no good, like the hot, destructive desert wind.

idiom: shake my head at you
meaning: A gesture of mocking scorn toward someone in trouble, sometimes with a show of pretended horror or surprise at their fate.

idiom: He gnashes His teeth at me
meaning: Grinding the teeth is a sign of fierce anger and hostility, like a wild beast about to tear its prey. In Job 16:9 it pictures the attacker raging against the sufferer.

idiom: I have buried my horn in the dust
meaning: The horn, as on a strong wild ox, stands for strength and power. Raising someone's horn means giving them strength, victory and honor over their enemies.

idiom: He has made me a byword among the people
meaning: God's dealings have turned Job into a common saying and topic of talk among people, his name used as shorthand for extreme misery or for someone who must have been very wicked; it marks him as an object of scorn and ridicule.

idiom: They have turned night into day
meaning: Most read it as Job's complaint about his friends: they pretended his dark time of suffering was really day and promised that good times were about to dawn. Others take it as Job's own sleepless misery, where night gives him no more rest than day does.

idiom: the gates of Sheol
meaning: The entrance to the underworld, the realm of the dead, thought of as a locked prison under the earth that no one leaves; going down there means dying, so Job's hope would die and be buried with him.

idiom: the lamp of the wicked is extinguished
meaning: The wicked man's prosperity, honor and happiness will come to an end; his home becomes dark and empty, and his good fortune does not pass on to his family. Some add an allusion to the hearth fire that welcomed guests, meaning he loses even the means to host others.

idiom: the lamp beside him goes out
meaning: His prosperity and that of his household comes to an end in complete desolation; homes kept a lamp burning all night, so its going out meant ruin.

idiom: the firstborn of death
meaning: The worst and deadliest disease that death produces, probably a wasting illness like Job's. As a firstborn was the strongest child, this is death's strongest offspring.

idiom: the king of terrors
meaning: Death, pictured as a fearsome ruler that the wicked are finally marched off to.

idiom: Will you never get enough of my flesh?
meaning: Job asks his friends why they keep tearing into him like hungry beasts. On top of his body's suffering, they wound him with endless accusations and slander, "eating his flesh" being an Eastern figure for maligning someone.

idiom: evil is sweet in his mouth and he conceals it under his tongue
meaning: The wicked man keeps evil and mischief stored behind his words, ready to bring out at any moment. Some sources compare it to a serpent's hidden poison or to malice hidden under smooth talk. One source reads it instead as a tasty morsel held in the mouth, meaning wickedness is to his taste.

idiom: the lamp of the wicked put out
meaning: The wicked man's prosperity, honor and happiness will come to an end; his home becomes dark and empty, and his good fortune does not pass on to his family. Some add an allusion to the hearth fire that welcomed guests, meaning he loses even the means to host others.

idiom: lift up your face to God
meaning: To face God openly; Ezra is too ashamed of the people's guilt to raise his face toward God.

idiom: His hand is heavy
meaning: God's afflicting hand presses hard on the sufferer, so his pain is greater than even his groaning shows. Some read the Hebrew in Job 23:2 as Job's own hand weighing on or holding back his groans, and the verse's wording is unclear.

idiom: injustice is broken like a tree
meaning: "Injustice" here stands for the unjust person. Like a tree that is broken and never grows again, the wicked person comes to an end and is forgotten. The sources differ on whether this is sudden or a quiet decay.

idiom: they are cut off like heads of grain
meaning: In this verse, to be destroyed or wiped out, as all living things were killed by the flood.

idiom: It claps its hands at him and hisses him out of his place
meaning: Clapping and hissing were public gestures of scorn and contempt; people mock the wicked man and are glad to see him fall and be driven away.

idiom: my steps were bathed in cream
meaning: An exaggerated picture of great abundance: in his prosperous days rich milk and oil were so plentiful that it was as if he walked in them wherever he went.

idiom: covered their mouths with their hands
meaning: They went silent out of respect and awe, stopping their talk and waiting to hear what Job would say.

idiom: my bow is renewed in my hand
meaning: The bow stands for strength and power; the speaker means his vigor never wore out but kept being renewed, so his ability and standing stayed fresh.

idiom: the light of my countenance
meaning: Job's kindly, cheerful face, a sign of his favor. People valued his smile so highly they could hardly believe he gave it, and nobody's gloom or opposition could take away his calm, bright look.

idiom: I have become a byword among them
meaning: Job has become the butt of the mockers' jokes and songs, his name passed around in their talk as a by-word for a hypocrite or wicked man, showing their contempt for him.

idiom: God has unstrung my bow
meaning: God has taken away Job's strength and means of defending himself, leaving him as useless as a bow with a slack string; with Job helpless, low people feel free to insult him. Some read the line instead as the rabble loosening their own reins, i.e. throwing off all restraint toward him.

idiom: I have become a brother of jackals, a companion of ostriches
meaning: His mournful cries sound like the howling of desert jackals and the wailing of ostriches. Like those animals he is left alone in desolation, with no one to pity him.

idiom: allowed the widow's eyes to fail
meaning: To let a widow look to him for help in vain until her hope wore out, disappointing her when she expected aid.

idiom: lifted up my hand against the fatherless
meaning: To threaten or strike down the defenseless orphan, using one's power and influence with the judges to oppress him.

idiom: if my land cries out against me and its furrows weep together
meaning: The land is personified as crying out to heaven for justice. Job means he never took land by fraud or force, never cheated its owners, and never wronged the workers who farmed it.

idiom: my belly is like unvented wine; it is about to burst like a new wineskin
meaning: The speaker is so full of things to say that he cannot hold them in any longer, like fermenting wine sealed in a skin with no outlet that is ready to split; he must speak to get relief.

idiom: nor will my hand be heavy upon you
meaning: Elihu promises not to overwhelm Job with pressure or harshness. He will treat him gently and not add to the weight of his suffering.

idiom: When He hides His face
meaning: God turns away and withholds his favor and help, in anger or seeming indifference. He acts as if he takes no notice of his people's suffering and does not step in to rescue them.

idiom: he claps his hands among us
meaning: A gesture of scornful triumph and defiance: Job is pictured mocking and acting as if he had won, rather than humbly submitting.

idiom: He seals up the hand of every man
meaning: God stops people's outdoor work with winter rain and snow, so that while they are forced to rest they recognize his power over them.

idiom: their upraised arm is broken
meaning: The power of the wicked, already raised to commit violence or oppression, is crushed and made useless.

idiom: tilt the water jars of the heavens
meaning: The rain-filled clouds are pictured as water skins that only God can control. Most read it as God tipping them to pour rain on the earth; some read it as God holding the rain back.

idiom: your own right hand can save you
meaning: Job's own strength would be enough to rescue him without God's help, proving he had the independent power to challenge God's rule; the point is that he does not.

idiom: I repent in dust and ashes
meaning: He shows complete humility and sorrow for his rash words by sitting in dust and ashes, the customary outward sign of grief and repentance.

idiom: Kiss the Son
meaning: A kiss was the customary way to pay homage and pledge loyalty to a king, so it means submitting to and honoring the king God has installed. Several sources reject the rendering "Son" and read it as pure homage to God, or as accepting instruction.

idiom: lifts my head
meaning: A head hangs down in grief and shame. Lifting it means God raises the person out of despair and humiliation, comforting them and restoring their honor.

idiom: Shine the light of Your face upon us
meaning: A request for God's favor and kindness, a prayer that He would look on the speaker with grace and show His presence; it echoes the priestly blessing of Numbers 6.

idiom: Their throats are open graves
meaning: The commentaries cover only the Ezekiel wording. There, God will bring his people, who are "dead" as a nation in exile, back to life and home to their land, as if raising them from their graves. The lands of exile are pictured as their graves. The sources do not explain "their throats are open graves."

idiom: fall by their own devices
meaning: Let their own schemes fail and turn back on them, so that their plots bring about their own downfall.

idiom: travails with evil
meaning: Like a woman in labor, the wicked man plans and strains to bring his harmful schemes to birth, but what he produces is falsehood and failure that comes back on himself.

idiom: under his tongue
meaning: The wicked man keeps evil and mischief stored behind his words, ready to bring out at any moment. Some sources compare it to a serpent's hidden poison or to malice hidden under smooth talk. One source reads it instead as a tasty morsel held in the mouth, meaning wickedness is to his taste.

idiom: He hides His face
meaning: God turns away and withholds his favor and help, in anger or seeming indifference. He acts as if he takes no notice of his people's suffering and does not step in to rescue them.

idiom: Lift up Your hand
meaning: A plea for God to take action and use His power, both to rescue the oppressed and to strike their oppressors.

idiom: incline Your ear
meaning: To incline the ear is to bend it toward someone and listen closely. It asks for, or trusts in, God's attentive hearing and answering of prayer, even the quiet sighs of the oppressed.

idiom: a double heart
meaning: Literally "a heart and a heart": speaking from one heart while hiding another, so saying one thing and meaning something else. It stands for deceit and insincerity, and sometimes for changing one's mind from day to day.

idiom: Give light to my eyes
meaning: Suffering was pictured as making the eyes dim. Brightened eyes meant renewed strength, life and gladness.

idiom: devour my people like bread
meaning: The wicked prey on God's people, robbing and ruining them as casually, greedily and routinely as they eat their daily meals, with no remorse; in effect they live off oppressing them.

idiom: my cup
meaning: A person's cup is their allotted share or condition in life; calling the Lord "my cup" means God Himself is the speaker's portion, the source of all he needs and enjoys.

idiom: The lines of my boundary have fallen in pleasant places
meaning: Taken from measuring cords used to mark out plots of land, which were then handed out by lot. The speaker means the portion he was given, his lot in life, is a good and pleasing one; for the psalmist that portion is above all God himself and life in God's presence.

idiom: at my right hand
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.

idiom: Incline Your ear to me
meaning: To incline the ear is to bend it toward someone and listen closely. It asks for, or trusts in, God's attentive hearing and answering of prayer, even the quiet sighs of the oppressed.

idiom: the apple of Your eye
meaning: The pupil of the eye, the most delicate and closely guarded part of the body; it stands for someone kept with the greatest care and tenderness, a deeply cherished object.

idiom: giving light to the eyes
meaning: Suffering was pictured as making the eyes dim. Brightened eyes meant renewed strength, life and gladness.

idiom: shake their heads
meaning: A gesture of mocking scorn toward someone in trouble, sometimes with a show of pretended horror or surprise at their fate.

idiom: hidden His face
meaning: God turns away and withholds his favor and help, in anger or seeming indifference. He acts as if he takes no notice of his people's suffering and does not step in to rescue them.

idiom: go down to the dust
meaning: To be heading for the grave. Most apply it to the poor and suffering who are close to dying, set against the rich; some widen it to all mortal people, and some report a reading that means those already dead.

idiom: lift up his soul to an idol
meaning: To set one's heart, desire, or devotion on something false or worthless, especially false gods, instead of being loyal to the true God.

idiom: Lift up your heads, O gates
meaning: Here it means Pharaoh called the two prisoners out and took up their cases to decide their fate. It works as a wordplay: one was raised back to his post, the other raised up to be hanged.

idiom: Hide not Your face
meaning: God turns away and withholds his favor and help, in anger or seeming indifference. He acts as if he takes no notice of his people's suffering and does not step in to rescue them.

idiom: pulled me up from Sheol
meaning: God saved the speaker when he was at the edge of death. He was as good as dead, so his recovery felt like being brought back from the realm of the dead.

idiom: hid Your face
meaning: God turns away and withholds his favor and help, in anger or seeming indifference. He acts as if he takes no notice of his people's suffering and does not step in to rescue them.

idiom: set my feet in the open
meaning: God gave him freedom and safety; instead of being trapped and handed over to his enemies, he was set loose with room to move and act.

idiom: out of mind
meaning: Completely forgotten, the way a dead man soon fades from people's memory and is no longer thought of.

idiom: Make Your face shine
meaning: A request for God's favor and kindness, a prayer that He would look on the speaker with grace and show His presence; it echoes the priestly blessing of Numbers 6.

idiom: cut off from Your sight
meaning: In a moment of panic the psalmist felt that God had abandoned him, that he was beyond God's notice and protection and as good as lost.

idiom: Your hand was heavy upon me
meaning: God's afflicting hand presses hard on the sufferer, so his pain is greater than even his groaning shows. Some read the Hebrew in Job 23:2 as Job's own hand weighing on or holding back his groans, and the verse's wording is unclear.

idiom: they gnashed their teeth at me
meaning: Grinding the teeth is a sign of fierce anger and hostility, like a wild beast about to tear its prey. In Job 16:9 it pictures the attacker raging against the sufferer.

idiom: wink in malice
meaning: Give one another a knowing wink, a sly signal of shared spite and gloating over the victim's downfall.

idiom: will be cut off
meaning: In this verse, to be destroyed or wiped out, as all living things were killed by the flood.

idiom: gnash their teeth at them
meaning: Grinding the teeth is a sign of fierce anger and hostility, like a wild beast about to tear its prey. In Job 16:9 it pictures the attacker raging against the sufferer.

idiom: the light of my eyes has faded
meaning: Suffering was pictured as making the eyes dim. Brightened eyes meant renewed strength, life and gladness.

idiom: made my days as handbreadths
meaning: A handbreadth was one of the smallest everyday measures. It means a human life is very short, close to nothing compared with God.

idiom: my ears You have opened
meaning: God has given the speaker ears ready to hear and obey His will; what God wants is attentive obedience rather than ritual sacrifice. Some read it as an allusion to piercing a slave's ear to mark lifelong service, which leads to the same idea of devoted obedience.

idiom: lifted up his heel against me
meaning: Like a horse that kicks the master who feeds it, or a wrestler who trips someone up. It means a trusted friend who shared his table turned on him in brutal betrayal.

idiom: Deep calls to deep
meaning: One trouble follows right after another, like waves or roaring torrents calling to each other, until the person is completely overwhelmed by a flood of afflictions.

idiom: the light of Your face
meaning: God's favor and loving-kindness toward His people, the opposite of His face being hidden.

idiom: a byword among the nations
meaning: To become a proverb that others point to: a people held up by the nations as a familiar example of calamity and of being forsaken by its God, and mocked in jeering sayings and songs.

idiom: spread out our hands to a foreign god
meaning: To pray to or worship another god, that is, to commit idolatry. Open, outstretched hands were the posture of prayer.

idiom: hide Your face
meaning: God turns away and withholds his favor and help, in anger or seeming indifference. He acts as if he takes no notice of his people's suffering and does not step in to rescue them.

idiom: grace has anointed your lips
meaning: The king's mouth and speech are full of charm, kindness and persuasive power, a gift poured on him from above that shows God's favor rests on him.

idiom: the oil of joy
meaning: Oil used to anoint people at feasts, weddings and other happy times, as opposed to mourning, when people did not anoint themselves. Being anointed with it means being given great joy and honor as a sign of God's favor. Christian commentators often apply it to the Messiah's exaltation or to the Spirit.

idiom: incline my ear
meaning: To listen closely; the psalmist first attends carefully to the wise saying he receives (from God) before setting it out for others.

idiom: see decay
meaning: To die and rot in the grave. To "not see decay" means to escape death and the grave.

idiom: Hide Your face from my sins
meaning: A plea for God to stop looking at the sins with anger, that is, to no longer hold them in view but to forgive and forget them.

idiom: They devour my people like bread
meaning: The oppressors destroy God's people as naturally and readily as they eat their ordinary food, without any thought of God.

idiom: go down to Sheol alive
meaning: To be cut off by a sudden, violent death in the middle of life, as if the earth opened and swallowed them alive like Korah's rebels. Sheol is the grave or realm of the dead, not the place of torment.

idiom: Put my tears in Your bottle
meaning: A plea for God to notice and remember every tear of sorrow, keeping them as something precious instead of letting them be forgotten. Some link this to the custom of keeping mourners' tears in small bottles. Others say it means a skin container that stores the tears like valued wine.

idiom: I will awaken the dawn
meaning: He means to get up before daybreak to praise God, as if his songs would wake the dawn instead of the dawn waking him. It is a poetic way of showing eager devotion.

idiom: stare down my foes
meaning: God will let him see what he longs for happen to his enemies: their plans fail and they are defeated, which means victory for him.

idiom: Moab is My washbasin
meaning: An expression of contempt and conquest: Moab is reduced to the lowliest household vessel, a basin for washing the feet, meaning it will be a subject people doing menial service.

idiom: upon Edom I toss My sandal
meaning: Edom will be conquered and humbled. Most sources picture it as the lowest slave, to whom a master throws his sandals to carry or clean. Others see a gesture of taking possession of land, or of trampling on a defeated enemy.

idiom: ride over our heads
meaning: God let enemies conquer and humiliate the people. They were trampled like beaten foes lying on the ground while the victor's horses and chariots drove over them.

idiom: the song of drunkards
meaning: Becoming a joke among drinkers and party-goers, who made up mocking songs about the speaker. It means being publicly ridiculed and the gossip of the town.

idiom: let not the Pit close its mouth over me
meaning: The edge of the grave: being right at the point of death, as if about to be swallowed by the world of the dead. In the psalm, scattered bones lying at Sheol's opening show people crushed, helpless and close to death.

idiom: May their table become a snare
meaning: A wish that the very comforts and good things of the enemies, their feasting and their sense of safety, would turn into the means of their sudden ruin, catching them like a baited trap.

idiom: lick the dust
meaning: Comes from the Eastern custom of lying face-down on the ground before a ruler; it means complete, humbled submission.

idiom: pride is their necklace
meaning: They show off their arrogance openly, wearing it like jewelry. The image is of a proud, stiff neck and a haughty bearing that everyone can see.

idiom: You hold my right hand
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.

idiom: withdraw Your strong right hand
meaning: The psalmist asks why God holds back his power and does not step in to help, as if he had tucked his hand idly inside the folds of his robe, and urges him to bring it out and act against the enemy.

idiom: Do not lift up your horn
meaning: The horn, as on a strong wild ox, stands for strength and power. Raising someone's horn means giving them strength, victory and honor over their enemies.

idiom: speak with an outstretched neck
meaning: To talk proudly, arrogantly, and defiantly, with the head held high in insolence.

idiom: All the horns of the wicked I will cut off
meaning: A horn stood for power and pride. God, or the speaker acting for him, would break the strength and arrogance of the wicked and take away their power to do harm.

idiom: the right hand of the Most High has changed
meaning: The right hand stands for God's power acting for his people. Some take the line as a lament that this helping power has changed, being held back or even turned against them; others read the key word as "years" and take it as a resolve to recall the years when God's power did great things for his people.

idiom: the bread of angels
meaning: The manna: food sent down from heaven, where angels live, and so fine it seemed fit for angels. The Hebrew literally says "bread of the mighty," which some take to mean food rich enough for princes.

idiom: twisted like a faulty bow
meaning: Unreliable, letting you down just when you need them. A faulty bow sends the arrow off course, drops it, or breaks, so the archer misses his target. Israel kept breaking its promises to God the same way.

idiom: into the laps of our neighbors
meaning: God will repay people fully and personally for their deeds. The picture is the loose fold of a robe over the chest, which people used like a pocket to carry things; the punishment is dropped right into it, in full measure and onto the guilty person.

idiom: cause Your face to shine upon us
meaning: A request for God's favor and kindness, a prayer that He would look on the speaker with grace and show His presence; it echoes the priestly blessing of Numbers 6.
