idiom: follow their own devices
meaning: As a punishment, God stopped restraining them and left them to their stubborn wills, so they lived by their own plans instead of his guidance, and it led to their ruin.

idiom: righteousness and peace have kissed
meaning: Righteousness and peace come together in full harmony, like friends embracing after being apart. It mainly describes qualities of God working together to save His people, and the people may reflect the same qualities.

idiom: I lift up my soul
meaning: To turn one's whole heart, desire and prayer toward God with sincere, eager devotion.

idiom: I spread out my hands
meaning: The posture of prayer: reaching his open hands toward God in earnest pleading for help.

idiom: our horn is exalted
meaning: The horn, as on a strong wild ox, stands for strength and power. Raising someone's horn means giving them strength, victory and honor over their enemies.

idiom: his horn will be exalted
meaning: The horn, as on a strong wild ox, stands for strength and power. Raising someone's horn means giving them strength, victory and honor over their enemies.

idiom: number our days
meaning: To weigh honestly how short and uncertain life is, so as to live wisely in light of it. Ellicott instead takes God as the one allotting the days, and reads it as a prayer that he make people know the power of his anger as he does so.

idiom: You have exalted my horn
meaning: The horn, as on a strong wild ox, stands for strength and power. Raising someone's horn means giving them strength, victory and honor over their enemies.

idiom: the abode of silence
meaning: The grave or the world of the dead, a place of stillness. Saying he would have dwelt there means he came close to dying.

idiom: whose hearts go astray
meaning: The people kept wandering from God at heart, morally lost by their own choice, and did not understand or follow his ways.

idiom: Do not hide Your face from me
meaning: God turns away and withholds his favor and help, in anger or seeming indifference. He acts as if he takes no notice of his people's suffering and does not step in to rescue them.

idiom: I have eaten ashes like bread
meaning: A picture of deep mourning: the sufferer sits in ashes as mourners did, so grief and humiliation have become his constant daily food.

idiom: My days are like lengthening shadows
meaning: Life is near its end: like an evening shadow that stretches longer as the sun goes down and then vanishes into night, the speaker's days are fading away.

idiom: stood before Him in the breach
meaning: To step into the broken spot in the wall and stand between the people and God's coming judgment, pleading for them or turning things around so the land is not destroyed, as Moses once did.

idiom: prostituted themselves by their deeds
meaning: To worship other gods or idols. Israel was seen as bound to God like a wife to a husband, so idolatry was treated as unfaithfulness in marriage. The phrase also fits the sexually impure rites that went with some pagan worship.

idiom: I am shaken off like a locust
meaning: He is weak and helpless, swept away by forces he cannot resist, the way the wind carries off a locust. His life is slipping away.

idiom: they shake their heads
meaning: A gesture of mocking scorn toward someone in trouble, sometimes with a show of pretended horror or surprise at their fate.

idiom: from the womb of the dawn
meaning: A picture of fresh, sudden abundance, like dew born at daybreak. Most apply it to the king's young warriors gathering to him eagerly, fresh and countless as morning dew. Others apply it to the king's own ever-renewed youthful strength.

idiom: the dew of Your youth
meaning: The sources disagree. Most say it means the king's young warriors coming to him eagerly, as fresh, sparkling and countless as morning dew. Others say it means the king's own youthful strength, always renewed. Some take it as a huge number of followers or offspring.

idiom: He will lift up His head
meaning: To stand erect in triumph; refreshed, the conquering king carries on to full victory and is exalted over his enemies.

idiom: his horn will be lifted high in honor
meaning: The horn, as on a strong wild ox, stands for strength and power. Raising someone's horn means giving them strength, victory and honor over their enemies.

idiom: he will gnash his teeth
meaning: The wicked man shows helpless rage, hatred and envy at seeing the righteous prosper.

idiom: I will lift the cup of salvation
meaning: The psalmist raises a cup, likely the drink offering that went with a thank offering, to give public thanks to God for rescuing him. Some read the cup as a figure for gladly receiving God's saving mercy, but either way it is an act of thanks for deliverance.

idiom: The right hand of the LORD performs with valor
meaning: God's power acts mightily, protecting His people and winning the victory, so the credit goes to Him and not to their own strength.

idiom: My soul cleaves to the dust
meaning: The speaker is crushed and brought very low, lying as if in the dust of death or deep humiliation and unable to rise; some also see a soul stuck to earthly things. He asks God to revive him.

idiom: You will enlarge my heart
meaning: God will set the heart free from what cramps and burdens it (fear, trouble, sin) and fill it with joy, love, and understanding, so the person can obey eagerly.

idiom: I have sought Your face
meaning: He earnestly pleaded for God's favor and presence, asking God to look kindly on him rather than turn away.

idiom: like a wineskin dried up by smoke
meaning: A leather wine bottle hung in a smoky house turns black, dry and shriveled. It pictures someone worn down and disfigured by suffering and grief.

idiom: You discard like dross
meaning: As a refiner throws away the worthless scum separated from metal, God removes the wicked and casts them off as useless.

idiom: Make Your face shine upon Your servant
meaning: A request for God's favor and kindness, a prayer that He would look on the speaker with grace and show His presence; it echoes the priestly blessing of Numbers 6.

idiom: the shade on your right hand
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.

idiom: whose quiver is full of them
meaning: Blessed with many sons. Sons are pictured as a warrior's arrows, so a full quiver means a large family of sons who give their father strength and protection against opponents.

idiom: The plowmen plowed over my back
meaning: A picture of cruel, drawn-out oppression of Israel, as if enemies had run a plow over its back. It recalls a lash cutting furrows into a slave's back. The long furrows mean the suffering was thorough and went on a long time.

idiom: like grass on the rooftops
meaning: Grass that sprouted in the thin soil of flat roofs soon dried up in the sun without ever ripening. It means something short-lived and useless, like enemies who perish before their plans come to anything.

idiom: I will make a horn grow for David
meaning: The horn, as on a strong wild ox, stands for strength and power. Raising someone's horn means giving them strength, victory and honor over their enemies.

idiom: like fine oil on the head
meaning: The sacred, fragrant anointing oil poured so generously on the high priest at his consecration that it ran down his beard to his collar; a picture of joy, fragrance, consecration and abundance, showing how delightful unity is and how it spreads over the whole people.

idiom: may my right hand cease to function
meaning: A solemn self-curse: if the speaker forgot Jerusalem (for example by playing joyful music in exile), may his right hand lose its skill, especially for playing the harp, or become useless altogether.

idiom: You have laid Your hand upon me
meaning: God holds the psalmist in His grip; he is always close at hand and under God's control, held up and held back, with no way to escape Him.

idiom: if I make my bed in Sheol
meaning: Sheol is the underworld or grave, the lowest place, set against heaven, the highest. Even if the psalmist lay down in the depths of the dead, God would be there. No place is beyond God's presence.

idiom: take Your name in vain
meaning: To misuse God's name for something empty or false. Some sources say it mainly forbids swearing a false oath in God's name; others say it also covers careless, frivolous, or insincere use, such as casual oaths, cursing, or magic.

idiom: It is oil for my head
meaning: Pouring oil on a guest's head was a refreshing, festive sign of welcome and honor. The psalmist will treat a godly person's rebuke as that kind of kindness, something that soothes and does good, not harm.

idiom: the mouth of Sheol
meaning: The edge of the grave: being right at the point of death, as if about to be swallowed by the world of the dead. In the psalm, scattered bones lying at Sheol's opening show people crushed, helpless and close to death.

idiom: whose right hands are deceitful
meaning: The right hand was raised when swearing an oath, so a lying right hand means people whose solemn oaths and pledges cannot be trusted.

idiom: He has raised up a horn for His people
meaning: The horn, as on a strong wild ox, stands for strength and power. Raising someone's horn means giving them strength, victory and honor over their enemies.

idiom: let us swallow them alive like Sheol
meaning: To be cut off by a sudden, violent death in the middle of life, as if the earth opened and swallowed them alive like Korah's rebels. Sheol is the grave or realm of the dead, not the place of torment.

idiom: incline your ear to wisdom
meaning: To listen eagerly and carefully to wisdom's teaching, giving it close attention.

idiom: incline your ear to my sayings
meaning: To bend down and listen carefully to the teacher's words because they matter greatly.

idiom: incline your ear to my insight
meaning: To listen attentively and fix the mind on the father's hard-won wisdom, much like "lend me your ears."

idiom: bitter as wormwood
meaning: The final outcome is extremely bitter and harmful. Wormwood was seen as both bitter and poisonous, so the pleasure at first ends in misery and ruin.

idiom: Drink water from your own cistern
meaning: Find sexual and emotional fulfillment only with your own wife, and stay faithful in marriage instead of going after another woman. The wife is pictured as a man's private water supply.

idiom: May your fountain be blessed
meaning: The "fountain" stands for a man's own wife; the wish is that she be blessed, mainly with children, and that he find his joy in her rather than in other women.

idiom: struck hands in pledge
meaning: To shake hands to seal a deal in which you promise to pay another person's debt if they fail; the proverb calls this rash.

idiom: you have fallen into your neighbor's hands
meaning: By guaranteeing another's debt you have put your freedom and property at that person's mercy, so you must act quickly and humbly to get released.

idiom: a little folding of the hands to rest
meaning: The pose of a lazy person who keeps his hands idle instead of working, which leads to his own ruin and poverty.

idiom: speaking with his feet
meaning: Making secret signals with the feet, such as shuffling, scraping, or pressing another's foot, to pass hidden messages to partners in a deceitful scheme.

idiom: as the apple of your eye
meaning: The pupil of the eye, the most delicate and closely guarded part of the body; it stands for someone kept with the greatest care and tenderness, a deeply cherished object.

idiom: Her house is the road to Sheol
meaning: Going into the adulteress's house leads to death and ruin (the grave, or hell itself); whatever route a man takes there, it ends in destruction.

idiom: He who winks the eye
meaning: A sly wink betrays secret malice, scheming with accomplices, or mockery, and it brings trouble on others.

idiom: will inherit the wind
meaning: Will end up with nothing. The man who harms his own household, whether by greed, harshness or bad management, gains nothing solid in the end, and what he has slips away.

idiom: the fruit of his lips
meaning: What a person says produces results. Good, wise and kind speech brings good things back to the speaker himself.

idiom: The light of the eyes
meaning: Most take it as the bright, joyful look in someone's eyes, which cheers whoever sees it; others take it as the light or pleasant sights the eyes take in.

idiom: he who purses his lips
meaning: Pressing or biting the lips is a facial sign of a sly, malicious person who has already settled on harm; some see it as a signal to partners in crime.

idiom: He who winks his eye
meaning: A sly wink betrays secret malice, scheming with accomplices, or mockery, and it brings trouble on others.

idiom: strikes hands in pledge
meaning: To shake hands to seal a deal in which you promise to pay another person's debt if they fail; the proverb calls this rash.

idiom: he who builds his gate high
meaning: He shows proud display, such as building a showy house to outshine others or beyond what he can afford, and so brings ruin on himself.

idiom: From the fruit of his mouth a man's belly is filled
meaning: A person lives with the results of their own words. What you say comes back to you, for good or bad, as surely as a harvest feeds the one who sowed it.

idiom: a wicked mouth swallows iniquity
meaning: To take in wrongdoing greedily and with pleasure, like a tasty morsel. The wicked enjoy doing evil and feed on it.

idiom: his lamp will be extinguished in deepest darkness
meaning: The wicked man's prosperity, honor and happiness will come to an end; his home becomes dark and empty, and his good fortune does not pass on to his family. Some add an allusion to the hearth fire that welcomed guests, meaning he loses even the means to host others.

idiom: The spirit of a man is the lamp of the LORD
meaning: The God-given human spirit, the breath of life from God that gives self-awareness and conscience, works like a lamp God has lit inside a person. It shines into the hidden depths of the heart and judges the person's thoughts and motives.

idiom: The king's heart is a waterway in the hand of the LORD
meaning: Just as a farmer steers irrigation water into whatever channel he wants, God steers even a king's will and decisions to serve His purposes.

idiom: A wicked man hardens his face
meaning: To put on a bold, shameless face: stubborn defiance that ignores rebuke, does not blush at sin and will not admit fault.

idiom: put a knife to your throat
meaning: Hold back your appetite with the strictest self-control when you eat at a ruler's table, as if a blade were at your throat. Some read it as a warning instead: overindulging there could cost you your life.

idiom: an adulteress is a narrow well
meaning: A pit with a narrow opening that is easy to fall into and very hard to climb out of. Getting involved with an adulteress traps a man in ruin he can hardly escape.

idiom: the lamp of the wicked will be extinguished
meaning: The wicked man's prosperity, honor and happiness will come to an end; his home becomes dark and empty, and his good fortune does not pass on to his family. Some add an allusion to the hearth fire that welcomed guests, meaning he loses even the means to host others.

idiom: heap burning coals on his head
meaning: Being kind to an enemy makes him burn with shame and regret, which may move him to repent. Others take it as the most effective kind of revenge, or as adding to God's judgment on him.

idiom: drinking violence
meaning: To bring a lot of harm, loss and shame on yourself. Sending a message by a fool means you end up swallowing the damage his blunders cause.

idiom: burning lips
meaning: Speech that glows with warm claims of love and friendship while hiding a wicked heart, a fine surface over something worthless. One source prefers a different reading: lips burning with malice and slander.

idiom: The wounds of a friend are faithful
meaning: A true friend's honest criticism may hurt, but it comes from real love and does you good. It is better than an enemy's many kisses, which are empty or false.

idiom: like holding back the wind or grasping oil with one's right hand
meaning: Trying to restrain a quarrelsome wife is hopeless; she can no more be held or hidden than the wind can be stopped or oil kept in a closed hand.

idiom: he who hides his eyes
meaning: He deliberately looks away from the poor, or pretends not to see them, so he will not have to feel pity or help.

idiom: gives light to the eyes
meaning: God gives the light of life to both poor and oppressor; both owe their existence to Him and depend on Him as maker and judge.

idiom: She eats and wipes her mouth
meaning: The adulteress commits her sin in secret, removes every trace of it the way someone wipes away signs of a meal, and then claims she is innocent. "Eating" is a polite way of referring to the sexual act.

idiom: She girds herself with strength
meaning: She prepares for her work with energy and determination, as people tucked up their long robes with a belt before hard work; strength is pictured as the belt she puts on.

idiom: her lamp is not extinguished at night
meaning: Most read it literally: the capable wife keeps working late into the night, so her lamp stays lit. Some take it as a picture of lasting prosperity, or of a life that stays bright.

idiom: under the sun
meaning: On earth, in this present world of human life and work. The phrase is used this way only in Ecclesiastes, and some sources compare it to similar Greek expressions and to the English word "sublunary."

idiom: nothing new under the sun
meaning: On earth, in this present world of human life and work. The phrase is used this way only in Ecclesiastes, and some sources compare it to similar Greek expressions and to the English word "sublunary."

idiom: folds his hands
meaning: The pose of a lazy person who keeps his hands idle instead of working, which leads to his own ruin and poverty.

idiom: he eats in darkness
meaning: He spends his whole life in gloom and misery, with no joy or light in his days.

idiom: those who see the sun
meaning: Living people, those who are alive under the sun.

idiom: go in and out
meaning: In this verse, going in and out of the holy place most likely means regularly frequenting the place of worship or seat of judgment, carrying on one's public life; the verse is read in many different ways.

idiom: Cast your bread upon the waters
meaning: Give freely and generously to others, especially the poor, even when it looks wasted and you can't expect anything back. In time the good you did will come back to you.

idiom: the silver cord is snapped
meaning: Death, when life finally comes apart. The picture is a precious lamp hung by a cord: the cord snaps, the lamp falls and breaks, and its light goes out. Some tie the cord to a body part such as the spine.

idiom: I will hide My eyes from you
meaning: God would refuse to take notice of them or pay any attention to their prayers.

idiom: strike hands
meaning: To join with others in a deal or pact; here Israel was making agreements and alliances (trade, marriage, or political) with foreign peoples and taking up their ways, which God's law forbade.

idiom: the breath in his nostrils
meaning: Human beings are frail and short-lived; their life hangs on a passing breath that can stop at any moment, so even powerful people are not worth relying on in place of God.

idiom: His hand is still upraised
meaning: God's anger is not satisfied yet and his punishment is not over. The blows already struck are only the start, and more judgment is still to come.

idiom: two smoldering stubs of firewood
meaning: The two hostile kings (Rezin of Aram and Pekah) are like the burnt-out ends of torches: they give off smoke but no real fire. They are nearly spent, they look more dangerous than they are, and they will soon go out, so there is no reason to fear them.

idiom: hiding His face
meaning: God turns away and withholds his favor and help, in anger or seeming indifference. He acts as if he takes no notice of his people's suffering and does not step in to rescue them.

idiom: the breath of His lips
meaning: The Lord overthrows his enemy with nothing more than what comes from his mouth (his breath or word), which shows his overwhelming power and how little effort it costs him. Some take it as the spoken gospel working over time, others as his power at his return, but either way his word alone is enough.

idiom: the rod of His mouth
meaning: The King's spoken word, acting like a ruler's scepter or a rod of punishment. His verdicts are so just and powerful that they strike down the wicked and oppressors with no other weapon needed.

idiom: all hands will fall limp
meaning: Hands hanging down helplessly: an image of terror and despair, losing all courage and strength to act or fight back.

idiom: every man's heart will melt
meaning: People lost all courage and hope from fear, as if their hearts had turned to water, leaving them no strength to act or resist.

idiom: His hand is outstretched
meaning: God's power is already at work to carry out what He has planned, and nobody can stop it or turn it aside.

idiom: The cornerstones of her tribes
meaning: Egypt's leading men or ruling class, the people the nation's whole structure rested on, the way a building rests on its cornerstones.

idiom: head or tail, palm or reed
meaning: Everyone in Egypt, from the highest rank to the lowest, is helpless; no one can do anything that works.

idiom: the key to the house of David
meaning: The badge of the top steward's office over the royal palace, meaning full authority over the king's household and affairs; he alone decided who got access.

idiom: like a peg into a firm place
meaning: Houses had strong pegs built into the walls to hang household goods on. It means a person firmly and securely set in office, someone his family and the nation can depend on.

idiom: Your hand is upraised
meaning: God's power has been plainly shown at work, protecting His people or punishing their enemies, but the wicked refuse to recognize it.

idiom: we gave birth to wind
meaning: All their painful effort and hopeful waiting produced nothing, like a pregnancy that ends with no child. They could not bring about deliverance on their own.

idiom: a covenant with death
meaning: A boast of false safety: people acting as if they had a deal with death and the grave that kept them from harm, while really trusting lies (likely a secret political alliance) rather than God.

idiom: You conceive chaff; you give birth to stubble
meaning: The enemy's plans and efforts will come to nothing, worthless like chaff and stubble, and their own rage will be what destroys them.

idiom: shakes her head behind you
meaning: Jerusalem mocks the Assyrian king with scornful gestures as he retreats in disgrace, as if to say his defeat was bound to happen.

idiom: turned his face to the wall
meaning: He turned away from the people around his couch to be alone with God, hiding his grief and praying in private.

idiom: I have rolled up my life like a weaver
meaning: Hezekiah sees his life ending early and suddenly, like a weaver rolling up a web and cutting it off the loom before it is finished. He expects to die within a day.

idiom: My righteous right hand
meaning: God's powerful hand that is faithful and dependable, acting in keeping with his faithfulness to his promises, which will hold up and protect his people.

idiom: takes hold of your right hand
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.

idiom: the hand of the LORD has done this
meaning: The change was clearly God's own work and power, so people would see Him as its author.

idiom: He feeds on ashes
meaning: He chases and delights in something worthless that cannot nourish him; worshiping an idol gives as much as a meal of ashes.

idiom: sit in the dust
meaning: To be brought down from power and luxury to the lowest humiliation, like a throneless captive or slave sitting on the ground; the posture was also linked with grief.

idiom: your neck is iron and your forehead is bronze
meaning: You are utterly stubborn, refusing God's yoke like an ox stiffening its neck, and shameless, never blushing at your sin.

idiom: My right hand
meaning: God's right hand stands for his power and greatness, here as the Creator who spread out and measured the heavens and so is able to save his people.

idiom: lick the dust at your feet
meaning: Comes from the Eastern custom of lying face-down on the ground before a ruler; it means complete, humbled submission.

idiom: Is My hand too short to redeem you
meaning: A shortened hand was a picture of weakness, and a long outstretched hand a picture of power. God asks whether his power has shrunk. It has not: he can still rescue his people as he did at the Exodus, so their troubles do not come from his weakness.

idiom: I have set My face like flint
meaning: He hardened himself with unshakable resolve and courage, so that shame, scorn, and suffering could not make him back down.

idiom: the rock from which you were cut
meaning: Abraham, the founding ancestor Israel came from (with Sarah as the "quarry"). The point: God made a great nation out of one old, childless couple, so he can surely restore his small, struggling people now.

idiom: the cup of staggering
meaning: To suffer the share of God's anger and punishment that is assigned to someone, pictured as a cup they are made to drink. In Jeremiah 49:12 the point is that if even God's own people were made to suffer it, Edom has no hope of escaping.

idiom: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news
meaning: Messengers who bring news of deliverance and salvation are a welcome, delightful sight, like a runner seen coming over the hills with good news. They are loved because of the message they carry.

idiom: bared His holy arm
meaning: God gets ready to act with force, like a warrior pulling back his sleeve or cloak to free his arm for battle. He steps in openly and powerfully for His people, where all nations can see it.

idiom: like sheep have gone astray
meaning: Like sheep with no shepherd, everyone has wandered away from God, each following his own selfish path toward danger and ruin.

idiom: I hid My face from you
meaning: God turns away and withholds his favor and help, in anger or seeming indifference. He acts as if he takes no notice of his people's suffering and does not step in to rescue them.

idiom: I am but a dry tree
meaning: The eunuch's complaint that he is barren: he can have no children or family line, and so (under the Law) no place or lasting share among God's people.

idiom: you have made your bed
meaning: Picture drawn from adultery: the people set up their altars and worshipped idols on the hilltops, being openly and shamelessly unfaithful to God as a wife betrays her husband; the "bed" stands for the place of idol worship.

idiom: hid My face
meaning: God turns away and withholds his favor and help, in anger or seeming indifference. He acts as if he takes no notice of his people's suffering and does not step in to rescue them.

idiom: turn your foot
meaning: To keep your feet off the Sabbath as if it were holy ground: no travel, ordinary business or pursuing your own affairs on that day.

idiom: ride on the heights of the land
meaning: To live in triumph, safety, and command, like a conqueror holding the high ground and strongholds of a country. In other words, to have full and secure possession of the land and a place of honor.

idiom: your sins have hidden His face from you
meaning: God turns away and withholds his favor and help, in anger or seeming indifference. He acts as if he takes no notice of his people's suffering and does not step in to rescue them.

idiom: drink the milk of nations
meaning: To be fed and enriched by the wealth and support of foreign nations and their kings, given freely to God's people the way a mother nurses a baby.

idiom: the oil of joy for mourning
meaning: Oil used to anoint people at feasts, weddings and other happy times, as opposed to mourning, when people did not anoint themselves. Being anointed with it means being given great joy and honor as a sign of God's favor. Christian commentators often apply it to the Messiah's exaltation or to the Spirit.

idiom: a crown of glory in the hand of the LORD
meaning: Zion would become something beautiful and precious to God, kept safe in His care and held up for the nations to admire as His work.

idiom: sworn by His right hand
meaning: God makes a solemn oath by his own power and strength (the hand that would be raised in oath-taking), pledging that might as the guarantee: as surely as he has power, the promise will be kept.

idiom: I have trodden the winepress alone
meaning: God (seen as the Messiah) has crushed his enemies in judgment single-handedly, with no human help. The winepress stands for the slaughter of battle, and the stains on his clothes are their blood.

idiom: hidden Your face from us
meaning: God turns away and withholds his favor and help, in anger or seeming indifference. He acts as if he takes no notice of his people's suffering and does not step in to rescue them.

idiom: smoke in My nostrils
meaning: These self-righteous people offend and anger God all the time, like smoke that stings the nose, or like the smoke of his own burning anger.

idiom: pay it back into their laps
meaning: God will repay people fully and personally for their deeds. The picture is the loose fold of a robe over the chest, which people used like a pocket to carry things; the punishment is dropped right into it, in full measure and onto the guilty person.

idiom: with your hands on your head
meaning: The gesture of grief, shame and despair. Judah will come away from Egypt disgraced and mourning because the help it counted on fails.

idiom: you have played the harlot
meaning: To worship other gods or idols. Israel was seen as bound to God like a wife to a husband, so idolatry was treated as unfaithfulness in marriage. The phrase also fits the sexually impure rites that went with some pagan worship.

idiom: remove the foreskins of your hearts
meaning: Put away the inner stubbornness, corrupt desires, and dullness toward God. Make real in the heart the purity and devotion to God that outward circumcision stood for.

idiom: had broken the yoke
meaning: The leaders threw off God's law and refused to obey, like oxen that break loose from the yoke and its straps and wander off.

idiom: our hands hang limp
meaning: Hands hanging down helplessly: an image of terror and despair, losing all courage and strength to act or fight back.

idiom: incline their ear
meaning: To listen with real attention; here the people would not give God even a partial hearing.

idiom: Is there no balm in Gilead?
meaning: Gilead was famous for a healing resin used on wounds, and for healers. The prophet asks in grief why there is no remedy and no healer for his people. Either the cure was there but not used, or no help could be found, and so the nation's wounds stay unhealed.

idiom: incline their ears
meaning: To bend the ear toward someone and really listen; the people refused to listen to and heed God's commands.

idiom: My heart would not go out to this people
meaning: God would not be favorably inclined toward them; even the greatest intercessors could not win his favor for them.

idiom: Her sun will set while it is still day
meaning: Disaster or death comes suddenly and too early, while she is still at the height of her prosperity and before the natural "evening" of life. It is a sudden fall from glory into shame, possibly pictured as an eclipse.

idiom: I will show them My back and not My face
meaning: God turns away and withholds his favor and help, in anger or seeming indifference. He acts as if he takes no notice of his people's suffering and does not step in to rescue them.

idiom: the ears of all who hear of it will ring
meaning: The news will be so shocking and terrible that anyone who hears it will be stunned, as if both ears had been struck.

idiom: I have set My face against this city
meaning: God turns toward someone with a fixed, hostile resolve. It means he is determined to oppose them in anger and bring punishment on them.

idiom: They strengthen the hands of evildoers
meaning: To encourage, support and enable people in their work; here the king's goodwill let them carry on and finish rebuilding the temple.

idiom: who wag their own tongues
meaning: Prophets who speak only from themselves, with no message from God, yet use the solemn formula "the LORD declares" so their own words pass as divine oracles.

idiom: go out of their minds
meaning: Struck by God's judgment through the sword, the nations reel and act wildly, like drunk men who have lost their reason from terror.

idiom: you will bring innocent blood upon yourselves
meaning: The guilt and responsibility for a person's death rests on that person (or on whoever is named), not on anyone else. Someone who dies through his own neglect or choice has only himself to blame.

idiom: The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the teeth of the children are set on edge
meaning: A popular saying that children were being punished for their parents' sins rather than their own. People used it to excuse themselves and to accuse God of unfairness. The prophet says it will be dropped because each person answers for their own wrongdoing.

idiom: his own teeth will be set on edge
meaning: A popular saying that children were being punished for their parents' sins rather than their own. People used it to excuse themselves and to accuse God of unfairness. The prophet says it will be dropped because each person answers for their own wrongdoing.

idiom: lay the iniquity of the fathers into the laps of their children
meaning: God lets the punishment and consequences of parents' sin, especially idolatry, fall on their descendants for several generations. Examples include disease, poverty, and bad example. This applies above all to children who keep on hating God and follow their fathers' ways.

idiom: I have hidden My face from this city
meaning: God turns away and withholds his favor and help, in anger or seeming indifference. He acts as if he takes no notice of his people's suffering and does not step in to rescue them.

idiom: I will set My face
meaning: God turns toward someone with a fixed, hostile resolve. It means he is determined to oppose them in anger and bring punishment on them.

idiom: their hands will hang limp
meaning: Hands hanging down helplessly: an image of terror and despair, losing all courage and strength to act or fight back.

idiom: his arm is broken
meaning: A nation's power and authority has been shattered, so it can no longer fight, rule, defend itself or attack others.

idiom: The horn of Moab has been cut off
meaning: Moab's strength, rule and pride have been destroyed, leaving the nation unable to attack or defend itself.

idiom: drink the cup
meaning: To suffer the share of God's anger and punishment that is assigned to someone, pictured as a cup they are made to drink. In Jeremiah 49:12 the point is that if even God's own people were made to suffer it, Edom has no hope of escaping.

idiom: his hands hang limp
meaning: Hands hanging down helplessly: an image of terror and despair, losing all courage and strength to act or fight back.

idiom: May my blood be on the dwellers of Chaldea
meaning: The guilt and responsibility for a person's death rests on that person (or on whoever is named), not on anyone else. Someone who dies through his own neglect or choice has only himself to blame.

idiom: He has cut off every horn of Israel
meaning: In his anger God took away all of Israel's strength, meaning its warriors, rulers, fortresses and every means of defense, so it could not resist the enemy.

idiom: gnash their teeth
meaning: Grinding the teeth is a sign of fierce anger and hostility, like a wild beast about to tear its prey. In Job 16:9 it pictures the attacker raging against the sufferer.

idiom: exalted the horn of your foes
meaning: The horn, as on a strong wild ox, stands for strength and power. Raising someone's horn means giving them strength, victory and honor over their enemies.

idiom: without a hand turned to help her
meaning: Sodom was destroyed in a moment by God alone, with no human hands at work against it. Jerusalem, by contrast, suffered long and cruelly at the hands of human enemies.

idiom: the breath of our life
meaning: The king, as the Lord's anointed, was the center of the nation's life. The people's survival and hopes as a nation depended on him, as much as life depends on breath.

idiom: the cup will pass to you
meaning: To suffer the share of God's anger and punishment that is assigned to someone, pictured as a cup they are made to drink. In Jeremiah 49:12 the point is that if even God's own people were made to suffer it, Edom has no hope of escaping.

idiom: at the risk of our lives
meaning: Getting food meant putting one's life in danger, here from raiding desert bands who attacked those bringing in the harvest or food.

idiom: the LORD's hand was upon him
meaning: God's power came over the prophet in inspiration, a force he could not resist that made him receive and pass on God's message.

idiom: I will make your face as hard as their faces
meaning: The image comes from horned animals butting heads. God would give the prophet a firmness and boldness greater than the stubbornness of the people, so he could face them without fear or shame.

idiom: the strong hand of the LORD upon me
meaning: God's powerful prophetic influence pressed on Ezekiel, pushing him on and holding him up so he carried out his mission despite his grief and anger.

idiom: the hand of the LORD was upon me
meaning: In this verse, being delivered out of the hand of the LORD means being spared the punishing judgment that would otherwise have fallen on the whole people.

idiom: set your face against the mountains of Israel
meaning: The prophet was to turn toward the land of Israel, perhaps literally facing that way, and aim his prophecy of judgment at it.

idiom: adulterous hearts
meaning: Hearts unfaithful to God that turned to idols. Worshiping idols is pictured as being unfaithful in a marriage (spiritual adultery).

idiom: the rod has budded, arrogance has bloomed
meaning: Judgment has fully grown and is ready to strike. Commentators split on what the rod is. Some take it as the proud Babylonian conqueror, the tool God would punish with, now grown to full strength. Others, playing on the fact that the word also means "tribe," take it as Judah, whose pride has grown until it is ripe for ruin.

idiom: every knee will turn to water
meaning: Total loss of strength and nerve from terror: legs trembling and giving way, with no power left to resist. Some note it may also refer to the sweat or loss of bladder control that fear causes.

idiom: I will turn My face away from them
meaning: God turns away and withholds his favor and help, in anger or seeming indifference. He acts as if he takes no notice of his people's suffering and does not step in to rescue them.

idiom: the hand of the Lord GOD fell upon me
meaning: God's power suddenly and forcefully seized the prophet, putting him into a trance or vision so he would receive God's message.

idiom: putting the branch to their nose
meaning: Probably a gesture from idol worship, perhaps holding a twig or bundle of branches up to the face while praying to the sun, as Persian sun-worshippers did. The custom is now unclear. Others take it as a gesture of scorn or an insult aimed at God.

idiom: The city is the cooking pot, and we are the meat
meaning: Jerusalem's leaders mocked the prophets' warnings: the city's walls would shield them from the enemy the way a pot keeps meat from the fire, so they were safe and judgment was not near. One commentator instead reads it as a grim saying of despair, that they were trapped and doomed to cook inside.

idiom: You did not go up to the gaps
meaning: To step into the broken spot in the wall and stand between the people and God's coming judgment, pleading for them or turning things around so the land is not destroyed, as Moses once did.

idiom: whitewashing any flimsy wall
meaning: The false prophets cover weak, unsound plans and false hopes of safety with approving words, making them look solid when they will collapse under God's judgment.

idiom: set your face against the daughters of your people
meaning: The prophet was to confront the false prophetesses openly and fearlessly, denouncing them so as to shame them.

idiom: puts a wicked stumbling block before his face
meaning: The sources explain only the wording "they are before My face": the people's sins are in full view of God. Nothing is hidden from Him, and He remembers them so that He can punish them.

idiom: I will set My face against them
meaning: God turns toward someone with a fixed, hostile resolve. It means he is determined to oppose them in anger and bring punishment on them.

idiom: I spread My cloak over you
meaning: The usual act of taking a woman as wife and putting her under protection; it pictures God marrying Israel in the covenant at Sinai.

idiom: played the harlot
meaning: To worship other gods or idols. Israel was seen as bound to God like a wife to a husband, so idolatry was treated as unfaithfulness in marriage. The phrase also fits the sexually impure rites that went with some pagan worship.

idiom: I will bring down upon his head My oath
meaning: Zedekiah had sworn his treaty with Babylon in God's name, so God counts the oath and covenant as his own. To bring them "upon his head" means God will make the oath-breaker himself bear the punishment for breaking them.

idiom: With an uplifted hand
meaning: Raising the hand toward heaven was the gesture for taking an oath, so the phrase means God swore a solemn oath and bound himself to his promise.

idiom: I will make you pass under the rod
meaning: A shepherd made his sheep pass under his staff to count and inspect them. God would count and examine his people, discipline them, and sort out the rebels, so that the rest would be brought back under the obligations of his covenant.

idiom: set your face toward the south
meaning: The prophet was to turn toward the land being addressed (Judah) and boldly, with determination, direct his message of judgment at it. This was also a sign that the Lord was set against it.

idiom: Every heart will melt
meaning: People lost all courage and hope from fear, as if their hearts had turned to water, leaving them no strength to act or resist.

idiom: their hearts may melt
meaning: People lost all courage and hope from fear, as if their hearts had turned to water, leaving them no strength to act or resist.

idiom: you shall be taken in hand
meaning: You will be seized and captured, handed over into the power of the enemy (the king of Babylon), caught as easily as a trapped bird.

idiom: your hands be strong
meaning: Will you still have the power to act and defend yourself when God judges you? The expected answer is no: courage would fail and hands would go limp.

idiom: stand in the gap
meaning: To step into the broken spot in the wall and stand between the people and God's coming judgment, pleading for them or turning things around so the land is not destroyed, as Moses once did.

idiom: she became a byword among women
meaning: To become a proverb that others point to: a people held up by the nations as a familiar example of calamity and of being forsaken by its God, and mocked in jeering sayings and songs.

idiom: you will not lift your eyes to them
meaning: You will no longer look to them with longing, whether to worship Egypt's idols or to seek help and alliance from Egypt.

idiom: You will drink your sister's cup
meaning: To suffer the share of God's anger and punishment that is assigned to someone, pictured as a cup they are made to drink. In Jeremiah 49:12 the point is that if even God's own people were made to suffer it, Edom has no hope of escaping.

idiom: the desire of your eyes
meaning: The person or thing someone loves and treasures most. For Ezekiel it was his wife, and she stood for the temple, which the people delighted in and were proud of.

idiom: the desire of their eyes
meaning: The person or thing someone loves and treasures most. For Ezekiel it was his wife, and she stood for the temple, which the people delighted in and were proud of.

idiom: set your face against the Ammonites
meaning: The prophet was to look toward the Ammonites' land with a stern, threatening expression and boldly announce judgment on them.

idiom: I will indeed expose the flank of Moab
meaning: Opening Moab's side (literally its shoulder) means leaving its border unprotected so that invaders can get in. The attack would come through its prized frontier cities, where its strength and pride lay.

idiom: The gate to the nations is broken
meaning: Jerusalem had been a gateway that the trade and traffic of many peoples passed through, and it stood between Tyre and that business. Now that it was destroyed, Tyre gloated that the commerce would come to her instead.

idiom: You were the seal of perfection
meaning: You were the very model of complete perfection, the finished pattern of wisdom and beauty (or a finely crafted signet ring of perfection); spoken with irony about how the king saw himself.

idiom: set your face against Sidon
meaning: The prophet was to turn his gaze and his words toward Sidon with a stern look and announce its coming ruin.

idiom: I will put hooks in your jaws
meaning: Pharaoh is pictured as a crocodile, the lord of the Nile, caught with hooks as crocodiles were. God would overpower him, drag him out of his safe place, and bring him to ruin, with his people and allies (the fish clinging to his scales) sharing his fall.

idiom: I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt
meaning: God has crushed Egypt's military power through defeat, and the injury will not be treated or healed, so Egypt can never take up the sword again.

idiom: set your face against Mount Seir
meaning: To turn toward Edom with a stern, hostile look and announce God's threats of judgment against it.

idiom: I have sworn with an uplifted hand
meaning: Raising the hand toward heaven was the gesture for taking an oath, so the phrase means God swore a solemn oath and bound himself to his promise.

idiom: we are cut off
meaning: The exiles' cry of despair: as a nation they are finished, severed like a limb or branch, with no hope of revival or return.

idiom: I will open your graves
meaning: The commentaries cover only the Ezekiel wording. There, God will bring his people, who are "dead" as a nation in exile, back to life and home to their land, as if raising them from their graves. The lands of exile are pictured as their graves. The sources do not explain "their throats are open graves."

idiom: set your face against Gog
meaning: The prophet was to face Gog boldly and fearlessly declare God's anger against him.

idiom: put hooks in your jaws
meaning: God will master Gog the way one controls a captured beast or a hooked fish, forcing him to go where God wants, which leads to his ruin.

idiom: I hid My face from them
meaning: God turns away and withholds his favor and help, in anger or seeming indifference. He acts as if he takes no notice of his people's suffering and does not step in to rescue them.

idiom: I will no longer hide My face from them
meaning: God turns away and withholds his favor and help, in anger or seeming indifference. He acts as if he takes no notice of his people's suffering and does not step in to rescue them.

idiom: uncircumcised in both heart and flesh
meaning: Put away the inner stubbornness, corrupt desires, and dullness toward God. Make real in the heart the purity and devotion to God that outward circumcision stood for.

idiom: uncircumcised in heart and flesh
meaning: Put away the inner stubbornness, corrupt desires, and dullness toward God. Make real in the heart the purity and devotion to God that outward circumcision stood for.

idiom: I swore with an uplifted hand
meaning: Raising the hand toward heaven was the gesture for taking an oath, so the phrase means God swore a solemn oath and bound himself to his promise.

idiom: God has numbered the days of your reign
meaning: God has fixed how long the kingdom would last, that time is now used up, and the reign is at its end.

idiom: cause Your face to shine upon Your desolate sanctuary
meaning: A request for God's favor and kindness, a prayer that He would look on the speaker with grace and show His presence; it echoes the priestly blessing of Numbers 6.

idiom: the Messiah will be cut off
meaning: The anointed one would be violently removed from among the living, usually read as being put to death. Most of these sources say this is Jesus, while Cambridge thinks it is the high priest Onias III.

idiom: I will break the bow of Israel
meaning: The bow was the main weapon of war and so stood for military might. Breaking it means God would shatter Israel's armed strength, which ended the northern kingdom, and this would happen in the Jezreel valley, the usual battlefield of the land.

idiom: Let her remove the adultery from her face and the unfaithfulness from between her breasts
meaning: Uses the picture of a prostitute who paints her face and shows off her breasts to lure lovers. Israel must give up the brazen, shameless signs of her idolatry, which was unfaithfulness to God.

idiom: has played the harlot
meaning: To worship other gods or idols. Israel was seen as bound to God like a wife to a husband, so idolatry was treated as unfaithfulness in marriage. The phrase also fits the sexually impure rites that went with some pagan worship.

idiom: They feed on the sins of My people
meaning: The priests lived off the sin offerings the people brought, so they profited from the people's wrongdoing and actually wanted them to sin more instead of correcting them; the Hebrew word means both "sin" and "sin offering."

idiom: they have played the harlot against their God
meaning: To worship other gods or idols. Israel was seen as bound to God like a wife to a husband, so idolatry was treated as unfaithfulness in marriage. The phrase also fits the sexually impure rites that went with some pagan worship.

idiom: The whirlwind has wrapped them in its wings
meaning: Israel will be carried off suddenly and with unstoppable force into exile in a distant land, as if swept up and away by a whirlwind.

idiom: you have been a snare at Mizpah, a net spread out on Tabor
meaning: Like hunters setting traps on these hills, the priests and rulers have lured and trapped the people into idolatry and wrongdoing across the land, east and west of the Jordan, when they should have been guarding them.

idiom: those who move boundary stones
meaning: Moving a neighbor's landmark was a cursed crime of taking what is not yours. The princes acted like such people, recklessly ignoring the limits of right set by God and the rights of others (some add literal land-grabbing or idolatry).

idiom: they are before My face
meaning: The sources explain only the wording "they are before My face": the people's sins are in full view of God. Nothing is hidden from Him, and He remembers them so that He can punish them.

idiom: Ephraim is an unturned cake
meaning: Through mixing with the pagan nations, Israel had become worthless, like a flat loaf left unturned on the coals: burnt on one side, raw on the other and fit for neither use. Most see an inconsistent people who claim to worship the LORD but follow pagan ways; Cambridge suggests a nation half-ruined by disasters.

idiom: Ephraim has hired lovers
meaning: Israel paid gifts and tribute to foreign powers such as Assyria to buy their friendship and help. This is pictured as a prostitute who pays her own lovers, which is unfaithfulness to God, her true husband.

idiom: you have played the harlot against your God
meaning: To worship other gods or idols. Israel was seen as bound to God like a wife to a husband, so idolatry was treated as unfaithfulness in marriage. The phrase also fits the sexually impure rites that went with some pagan worship.

idiom: My heart is turned within Me
meaning: God's feelings are overturned, turning from anger to pity: deep compassion wins out over the punishment Israel deserved, so He will not destroy them completely.

idiom: Ephraim feeds on the wind and pursues the east wind
meaning: Israel was living on empty hopes, mainly foreign alliances and idols, which could not sustain it. Worse, it was chasing something that would actually destroy it, like the scorching desert east wind.

idiom: Where, O Death, are your plagues? Where, O Sheol, is your sting?
meaning: Most sources read it as a triumphant taunt over a defeated enemy: death and the grave have lost their power to hurt God's people, whom He will rescue. Others read it as God calling on death and Sheol to bring out their plagues and strike rebellious Israel.

idiom: the fruit of our lips
meaning: What the lips produce, meaning words of confession, praise and thanks given to God as an offering in place of animal sacrifices.

idiom: For three transgressions of Damascus, even four
meaning: Not an exact count. It is a stock Hebrew rising-number saying for many repeated sins, with the last one pushing the guilt past the limit, so God's judgment will not be called back.

idiom: For three transgressions of Gaza, even four
