idiom: For three transgressions of Israel, even four
meaning: Not an exact count. It is a stock Hebrew rising-number saying for many repeated sins, with the last one pushing the guilt past the limit, so God's judgment will not be called back.

idiom: I destroyed his fruit above and his roots below
meaning: God wiped the Amorites out completely, root and branch. Both their offspring and the stock that could have produced more were destroyed.

idiom: you cows of Bashan
meaning: Bashan's rich pastures produced fat, well-fed cattle. The phrase scorns Samaria's pampered, self-indulgent rich, who care only for their own comfort while they oppress the poor. Most take it of the wealthy women, some of the effeminate nobles.

idiom: cleanness of teeth
meaning: Famine: teeth stay clean because there is no food to eat.

idiom: like a firebrand snatched from a blaze
meaning: A charred stick pulled out of the fire just in time; a narrow escape from complete destruction, though not without damage.

idiom: turn justice into wormwood
meaning: To twist justice, which should be sweet and healing, into something bitter and cruel for those who receive it, through corrupt judgment and oppression.

idiom: the fallen tent of David
meaning: David's royal house and kingdom, brought down from a palace to something like a broken-down hut. God promises to rebuild it, a promise many link to the Messiah.

idiom: Those who eat your bread
meaning: Close, trusted friends and allies who share your table, a bond held sacred in Eastern culture, who would still betray you and set a trap.

idiom: so all the nations will drink continually
meaning: To suffer the share of God's anger and punishment that is assigned to someone, pictured as a cup they are made to drink. In Jeremiah 49:12 the point is that if even God's own people were made to suffer it, Edom has no hope of escaping.

idiom: the belly of Sheol
meaning: A vivid picture of being as good as dead, swallowed into the world of the dead with no apparent way out.

idiom: cannot tell their right hand from their left
meaning: Describes young children too young to tell even basic things apart, and so not yet able to judge right from wrong or be held morally responsible.

idiom: the Daughter of Zion
meaning: A poetic name for the people of Jerusalem (Zion), pictured as a woman.

idiom: make yourselves as bald as an eagle
meaning: A call to mourn as deeply as possible: shaving the head was a common sign of grief, and making it as bare as the bald-headed vulture (or a moulting eagle) meant grief beyond the usual, here for children taken away into exile.

idiom: a disaster from which you cannot free your necks
meaning: A punishment pictured as a heavy yoke on the neck, like one put on cattle, that cannot be shaken off. It means conquest and exile under foreigners, which would also bring their proud, raised heads low.

idiom: they will take up a proverb against you
meaning: Enemies would make a mocking taunt-song out of Israel's own mournful lament, repeating it back in scorn.

idiom: a man of wind
meaning: A false prophet whose message is as empty and worthless as wind, who tells people the pleasant lies they want to hear, such as promises of plenty and good living.

idiom: He will hide His face from them
meaning: God turns away and withholds his favor and help, in anger or seeming indifference. He acts as if he takes no notice of his people's suffering and does not step in to rescue them.

idiom: who proclaim peace while they chew with their teeth
meaning: Prophets for hire: as long as people feed or pay them, they predict peace and good times, but they threaten war and disaster against anyone who gives them nothing. Some read "bite" as a serpent's bite, meaning they do deadly harm while promising peace.

idiom: They will all cover their mouths
meaning: Covering the upper lip and beard was a sign of shame and mourning (also required of lepers); the false prophets would be silenced and humiliated because God gave them no answer.

idiom: walk in the name of their gods
meaning: To shape one's whole life and conduct around one's god, staying loyal to it and relying on its power and protection. The nations do this with their worthless gods, while Israel lives in steady loyalty to the LORD and draws its strength from Him.

idiom: let us feast our eyes on Zion
meaning: To gaze at Zion's ruin and humiliation with spiteful pleasure.

idiom: I will give you horns of iron and hooves of bronze
meaning: Zion is pictured as an ox at threshing, goring with its horns and trampling with its hooves. God promises to make his people strong enough to knock down and crush the nations gathered against them.

idiom: seven shepherds, even eight leaders of men
meaning: A full and more-than-enough number of capable leaders; seven stands for a complete number and adding eight means even more than needed, so God will raise up plenty of rulers to drive back the invader.

idiom: They will lick the dust like a snake
meaning: Comes from the Eastern custom of lying face-down on the ground before a ruler; it means complete, humbled submission.

idiom: Hearts melt, knees knock
meaning: People lost all courage and hope from fear, as if their hearts had turned to water, leaving them no strength to act or resist.

idiom: I will lift your skirts over your face
meaning: This was the worst possible insult: an exposed harlot or a captive woman was shamed by having her robes pulled up. God would strip proud Nineveh of its glory and lay its shame open for every nation to see.

idiom: they are like your women
meaning: Nineveh's soldiers, once fierce, will be struck with panic and too weak and scared to fight off the invaders. The sources call this a common taunt of the time.

idiom: your shepherds slumber
meaning: Your leaders and officials are asleep, most say in the sleep of death (slain), others say careless and inactive; either way the people are left leaderless and scattered.

idiom: He enlarges his appetite like Sheol
meaning: His greed, especially for conquest, has no limit, like the grave, which takes in everyone and is never full.

idiom: to place his nest on high
meaning: Like an eagle nesting out of reach, to use ill-gotten wealth to make one's house or dynasty secure and untouchable by danger, a sign of pride and self-reliance.

idiom: the stones will cry out from the wall
meaning: Even the building materials of a house or empire built with stolen wealth and forced labor will act as witnesses. They accuse the builder of his injustice and call down judgment on him.

idiom: The cup in the LORD's right hand will come around to you
meaning: The cup stands for God's judgment and wrath, which had been passed around to the nations; now it comes to the oppressor in turn, so that he suffers the same shame he inflicted on others.

idiom: Her princes are roaring lions; her judges are evening wolves
meaning: The city's rulers and judges, who should protect the people, prey on them instead. Like starving beasts they are violent and greedy, and they devour the poor completely and at once, leaving nothing behind.

idiom: they rose early to corrupt all their deeds
meaning: They did evil eagerly and on purpose, wasting no time and putting all their effort into it, like people who get up at dawn to start important work.

idiom: I will restore pure lips to the peoples
meaning: The nations' lips were unclean from calling on false gods. God would cleanse them so they could call on the LORD alone. "Shoulder to shoulder" pictures animals pulling under one yoke, meaning all would serve him together with one mind.

idiom: O Daughter of Zion
meaning: A poetic name for the people of Jerusalem (Zion), pictured as a woman.

idiom: do not let your hands fall limp
meaning: Hands hanging down helplessly: an image of terror and despair, losing all courage and strength to act or fight back.

idiom: I will make you like My signet ring
meaning: A signet ring was precious, carefully kept, worn close, and used to carry its owner's authority. God would treasure and protect Zerubbabel and give him authority as his chosen representative. This reverses the rejection of Jeconiah, whom God had pulled off "like a signet."

idiom: lifted up their horns against the land of Judah
meaning: A horn stood for strength and power. Lifting it means nations proudly using their power to attack and crush Judah.

idiom: whoever touches you touches the apple of His eye
meaning: The pupil of the eye, the most delicate and closely guarded part of the body; it stands for someone kept with the greatest care and tenderness, a deeply cherished object.

idiom: I will surely wave My hand over them
meaning: Shaking the hand over a nation was a threatening gesture. One wave of God's hand is enough to strike down his people's enemies, and those who once plundered and enslaved others would become plunder for their own former servants.

idiom: sit under your own vine and fig tree
meaning: A picture of peaceful, safe, prosperous life, like the days of Solomon, with neighbors gathering and enjoying friendly company together.

idiom: What are you, O great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you will become a plain.
meaning: However huge the obstacles and opposition to rebuilding the temple seem, they will be leveled and disappear before Zerubbabel. Leveling mountains was a proverbial way of describing the overcoming of the hardest difficulties.

idiom: the day of small things
meaning: A time of humble, unimpressive beginnings, like the modest start on rebuilding the temple. It should not be looked down on, because God watches over the work with favor and will see it finished.

idiom: Let your hands be strong
meaning: To encourage, support and enable people in their work; here the king's goodwill let them carry on and finish rebuilding the temple.

idiom: O prisoners of hope
meaning: Captives who are still held but not without hope, because God's covenant promise of deliverance still stands for them; they are called to return to their place of safety.

idiom: I will bend Judah as My bow
meaning: God pictures himself as a warrior who uses his own people as his weapons, Judah as the bow he draws and Ephraim as the arrow he shoots. The point is that Israel would fight and beat its enemies (Greece) only in God's strength and by his will, not in its own power.

idiom: The cornerstone will come from Judah, the tent peg from him
meaning: Judah would no longer depend on foreign rulers. From its own people would come a chief ruler that holds the nation together (the cornerstone), steady leaders that others can rely on (the peg), military strength, and every kind of leader it needs. Many also see the Messiah here.

idiom: this magnificent price at which they valued me
meaning: Bitter irony: the thirty silver pieces were an insultingly small wage (about the price of a slave), showing how little they valued the shepherd. It was fit only to be thrown to the potter.

idiom: I will make Jerusalem a cup of drunkenness
meaning: To suffer the share of God's anger and punishment that is assigned to someone, pictured as a cup they are made to drink. In Jeremiah 49:12 the point is that if even God's own people were made to suffer it, Edom has no hope of escaping.

idiom: living water will flow out from Jerusalem
meaning: In everyday speech it meant flowing spring water, not still water. Jesus used it for the life-giving grace and Spirit He gives, which truly satisfies the soul.

idiom: but Esau I have hated
meaning: God did not choose Esau and his descendants, Edom, for the special favor He gave Jacob, and in that sense rejected him. This is relative rather than active hatred: Edom was left in ruin while Israel was restored.

idiom: He who divorces his wife covers his garment with violence
meaning: Divorcing one's wife is a cruel wrong that marks the man, clinging to him as plainly as his clothing. Sources disagree on what the garment is: his own outward clothing or character, his wife, the protection he owed her, or a cover for his wrongdoing.

idiom: the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings
meaning: God's justice, appearing on the day of judgment, will dawn on the faithful like the rising sun. Its rays (the "wings") bring healing, relief and joy, and clear away the confusion and injustice they have suffered. Many apply it to the Messiah.

idiom: before they came together
meaning: Before the betrothed couple began living together as husband and wife, meaning before he took her into his home and before they had sexual relations.

idiom: whose sandals I am not worthy to carry
meaning: Carrying, tying and untying a master's sandals was the job of the lowest household slave. John means he is not fit to be even the humblest servant of the one coming after him.

idiom: His winnowing fork is in His hand
meaning: The coming Messiah is ready to sort the good from the bad, just as a farmer tosses threshed grain into the wind to separate wheat from chaff. He will gather the righteous safely and destroy the worthless, ending the present mixture of the two.

idiom: the poor in spirit
meaning: People who are humble inside and know they have nothing of their own to offer God. They feel their need, rely on his mercy and do not trust in themselves; they are the opposite of the spiritually proud. Luke's shorter form points to the literally poor, but Matthew's wording is not limited to them.

idiom: not a single jot, not a stroke of a pen
meaning: Not even the smallest detail of the Law, down to its tiniest letter or the smallest mark on a letter, will be lost until all it was meant to do has happened.

idiom: if your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away
meaning: Strict self-denial: give up even your most valued abilities or possessions, which a right hand stands for, if they draw you into sin, because losing them is better than being lost.

idiom: Eye for eye and tooth for tooth
meaning: The law that the penalty must match the injury, no more and no less. It was a rule for judges and courts, not a license for personal revenge, and was often settled by a matching payment rather than literal maiming.

idiom: go with him two miles
meaning: If an official or soldier forces you into service, such as carrying a load for a mile, willingly do twice as much instead of resisting or quarreling, for the sake of peace.

idiom: do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing
meaning: A proverbial exaggeration for giving in complete secrecy, without show and without even dwelling on it oneself.

idiom: forgive us our debts
meaning: Sins are pictured as debts owed to God: failing to give him what is due, which leaves us owing a penalty we cannot pay. The prayer asks God to cancel that debt, as we have forgiven those who wrong us. Calling sins "debts" was common Jewish usage.

idiom: If your eyes are good
meaning: The eye is the body's lamp. A good (sound, single) eye stands for an inner sight fixed steadily on one goal, God and heavenly treasure, and that lights up the whole life. Gill instead uses the Jewish idiom in which a good eye means a generous spirit and an evil eye a stingy one.

idiom: The eye is the lamp of the body
meaning: Just as the eye lets light in and guides the whole body, a person's inner outlook (mind, conscience or heart) guides their whole life. If that inner eye is clear and fixed on God alone, the whole life is filled with light. One source takes a good eye to mean a generous spirit, in line with Jewish usage.

idiom: if your eyes are bad
meaning: The eye is the body's lamp. A good (sound, single) eye stands for an inner sight fixed steadily on one goal, God and heavenly treasure, and that lights up the whole life. Gill instead uses the Jewish idiom in which a good eye means a generous spirit and an evil eye a stingy one.

idiom: weeping and gnashing of teeth
meaning: Grinding the teeth is a sign of fierce anger and hostility, like a wild beast about to tear its prey. In Job 16:9 it pictures the attacker raging against the sufferer.

idiom: let the dead bury their own dead
meaning: A play on two meanings of "dead": let those who are spiritually dead, and have no interest in God's kingdom, handle burying the physically dead. Following Christ must come before even the most sacred family duty.

idiom: No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment
meaning: Joining something new to something old does not fit and only makes the damage worse. Some take it that Jesus' teaching is not a patch to mend the old religious system; others that strict duties such as fasting should not be imposed on disciples not yet ready for them.

idiom: Neither do men pour new wine into old wineskins
meaning: Something new and vigorous needs a fitting container, or both are lost. Some take it that Jesus' new teaching cannot be forced into the old forms of the religion of the day or into people still bound to them; others that new spiritual gifts and demands should not be pressed suddenly on people not yet ready, but given gradually.

idiom: let your peace rest on it
meaning: Your greeting and blessing of peace will take effect on a receptive, peace-loving person; if there is none, the blessing comes back to you with no effect on them.

idiom: shake the dust off your feet
meaning: A public sign of breaking off from a place that rejected God's messengers; Jews shook off the dust of pagan lands as unclean, so doing this to a Jewish town treated it as no better than heathen, cut all ties, and left it responsible for its own guilt.

idiom: We played the flute for you, and you did not dance
meaning: Taken from children in the marketplace who play at weddings and funerals and complain that their sulky friends join neither game. It describes people who cannot be pleased whatever is offered: they rejected John's strict, mournful way and also Jesus' joyful, ordinary way of living.

idiom: in sackcloth and ashes
meaning: Sackcloth was rough, coarse cloth worn in mourning, and people put ashes on their heads to show grief. Repenting in sackcloth and ashes means turning from sin with deep, outwardly shown sorrow.

idiom: My yoke is easy and My burden is light
meaning: What Jesus asks of his followers is kind and not crushing, unlike the heavy demands of the law and the added rules of the religious teachers; it brings rest rather than strain.

idiom: It is not right to take the children's bread and toss it to the dogs
meaning: A common saying of the time: the "children" were the Jews, God's people, and "dogs" was a scornful name for Gentiles. It meant the blessings meant first for Israel should not be handed to outsiders ahead of them. Jesus used it to test the woman's faith, not to approve the insult.

idiom: Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees
meaning: Watch out for the Pharisees' corrupting influence, which Luke names as hypocrisy, a show of holiness that isn't real. Like yeast, it works unseen and slowly spreads until it affects everything.

idiom: the gates of Hades will not prevail against it
meaning: Neither the power of death and the grave nor the forces of evil will overcome or destroy the church. It will never perish.

idiom: Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven
meaning: In Jewish usage, "binding" and "loosing" meant declaring something forbidden or allowed. The apostles are given authority to rule on what is required or permitted in the church, and to admit or exclude people, and heaven will confirm those decisions.

idiom: If your hand or your foot causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away
meaning: Firmly give up anything that leads you into sin, whether pursuits, possessions or friendships, however dear. Going to life without them is better than keeping them and being lost.

idiom: may sit at Your right hand, and the other at Your left
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.

idiom: Can you drink the cup I am going to drink?
meaning: Jesus asks if they can endure the bitter suffering God has given him. In Scripture a cup is a person's appointed lot, often affliction or God's wrath.

idiom: You will indeed drink My cup
meaning: Jesus tells James and John they will share in his suffering. James was later killed for his faith, and John suffered persecution and exile.

idiom: sit in Moses' seat
meaning: To hold the recognized authority to teach and explain the Law of Moses, as his successors in that role; Jewish teachers sat down when they explained Scripture.

idiom: twice as much a son of hell as you are
meaning: "Son of hell" was a Hebrew way of saying someone deserved Gehenna, that is, was thoroughly wicked. Jesus says the Pharisees' converts end up twice as bad as their teachers: they pick up their teachers' hypocrisy and vices on top of their old pagan ones, and they often push the new creed's worst features to extremes.

idiom: You strain out a gnat but swallow a camel
meaning: A proverb for being fussy over the tiniest points of the law while ignoring huge sins; strict Jews filtered drinks to avoid swallowing a tiny unclean insect, yet these leaders took in something as large and unclean as a camel.

idiom: You are like whitewashed tombs
meaning: Tombs were whitewashed each year so people would see them and avoid touching them and becoming ritually unclean. They looked bright outside but held decay inside, just as the Pharisees looked holy but were inwardly corrupt.

idiom: Fill up, then, the measure of the sin of your fathers
meaning: Ironic permission that is really a prediction: go ahead and finish the evil your ancestors began, by killing Christ and his messengers, until the full limit of guilt is reached and God's punishment falls.

idiom: Wherever there is a carcass, there the vultures will gather
meaning: A proverb: just as vultures surely and quickly find a dead body, judgment will surely arrive wherever corruption is. Many apply it to the Roman armies descending on corrupt Jerusalem. Others apply it to God's agents of destruction in general, to everyone gathering before Christ for judgment, or to the certainty of recognizing His coming.

idiom: The one who has dipped his hand into the bowl with Me
meaning: Someone sharing the same dish at the meal, a close table companion. In Eastern eyes, eating together made a betrayal all the more monstrous. Some see it also as a pointer to Judas, who sat near Jesus.

idiom: let this cup pass from Me
meaning: To suffer the share of God's anger and punishment that is assigned to someone, pictured as a cup they are made to drink. In Jeremiah 49:12 the point is that if even God's own people were made to suffer it, Edom has no hope of escaping.

idiom: if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it
meaning: The "cup" means the portion or lot God assigns to a person; here Jesus asks to be spared the suffering ahead of him, while yielding to the Father's will.

idiom: sitting at the right hand of Power
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.

idiom: His blood be on us and on our children
meaning: The guilt and responsibility for a person's death rests on that person (or on whoever is named), not on anyone else. Someone who dies through his own neglect or choice has only himself to blame.

idiom: who had fallen asleep
meaning: To have died. Sleep is the usual gentle picture for death, especially a believer's death.

idiom: He is out of His mind
meaning: His family thought He had lost control of Himself, carried away by intense zeal and overwork; it was a disturbed state rather than outright insanity.

idiom: Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod
meaning: Watch out for the Pharisees' corrupting influence, which Luke names as hypocrisy, a show of holiness that isn't real. Like yeast, it works unseen and slowly spreads until it affects everything.

idiom: If your hand causes you to sin, cut it off
meaning: Not meant literally: give up anything that leads you into sin, even something as dear and useful as a hand, whether a habit, a pleasure or a close friend. Any loss is better than ending in hell.

idiom: If your foot causes you to sin, cut it off
meaning: The same figure: cut yourself off from anything, even people or things you depend on for support, that leads you into sin, because losing them is better than being lost.

idiom: everyone will be salted with fire
meaning: Many read it as fiery trial and self-denial that purify Christ's followers and make them acceptable to God, like salt on a sacrifice. Others read it as the wicked being kept from being consumed in unending punishment, the way salt preserves. Some apply it to both.

idiom: Have salt among yourselves
meaning: Keep within you the purifying, preserving quality that salt stands for (grace, self-denial, freedom from selfish ambition). Because shared salt was also a sign of covenant and friendship, this goes together with living in peace rather than rivalry.

idiom: sit at Your right hand and the other at Your left
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.

idiom: Can you drink the cup I will drink
meaning: The cup is the portion God has set out for someone, taken from the host at a feast who serves each guest a share. Here it is Jesus' coming suffering, and he asks if they can bear it with him.

idiom: You will drink the cup that I drink
meaning: The brothers would go through suffering for Jesus' sake, something like his own, as they later did through martyrdom and persecution.

idiom: the one who is dipping his hand into the bowl with Me
meaning: Someone sharing the same dish at the meal, a close table companion. In Eastern eyes, eating together made a betrayal all the more monstrous. Some see it also as a pointer to Judas, who sat near Jesus.

idiom: Take this cup from Me
meaning: The "cup" means the portion or lot God assigns to a person; here Jesus asks to be spared the suffering ahead of him, while yielding to the Father's will.

idiom: sat down at the right hand of God
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.

idiom: a horn of salvation
meaning: The horn, as on a strong wild ox, stands for strength and power. Raising someone's horn means giving them strength, victory and honor over their enemies.

idiom: the Dawn will visit us from on high
meaning: The coming of the Messiah is pictured as a sunrise sent from heaven. Out of God's deep mercy, light breaks into the darkness people live in.

idiom: poured into your lap
meaning: To be given a generous return, handed right to you. The "lap" is the large fold of a robe over the chest, which people used as a pocket. The measure is pictured as grain pressed down and overflowing.

idiom: fall away
meaning: To stumble over Jesus: to be put off by him, or by the way he came and acted, and so to doubt or reject him.

idiom: wisdom is vindicated by all her children
meaning: God's wisdom is shown to be right by those who truly follow it. People who accepted both John's strict way and Jesus' open way prove that God's methods were sound, even though others found fault with both.

idiom: they fall away
meaning: Shallow believers give up their faith and abandon the message when hardship or persecution tests them.

idiom: your peace will rest on him
meaning: Your greeting and blessing of peace will take effect on a receptive, peace-loving person; if there is none, the blessing comes back to you with no effect on them.

idiom: the dust of your town that clings to our feet, we wipe off
meaning: A public sign of breaking off from a place that rejected God's messengers; Jews shook off the dust of pagan lands as unclean, so doing this to a Jewish town treated it as no better than heathen, cut all ties, and left it responsible for its own guilt.

idiom: sitting in sackcloth and ashes
meaning: Sackcloth was rough, coarse cloth worn in mourning, and people put ashes on their heads to show grief. Repenting in sackcloth and ashes means turning from sin with deep, outwardly shown sorrow.

idiom: Your eye is the lamp of your body
meaning: Just as the eye lets light in and guides the whole body, a person's inner outlook (mind, conscience or heart) guides their whole life. If that inner eye is clear and fixed on God alone, the whole life is filled with light. One source takes a good eye to mean a generous spirit, in line with Jewish usage.

idiom: the leaven of the Pharisees
meaning: Watch out for the Pharisees' corrupting influence, which Luke names as hypocrisy, a show of holiness that isn't real. Like yeast, it works unseen and slowly spreads until it affects everything.

idiom: to ignite a fire on the earth
meaning: Sources differ on what the fire is: judgment that purifies and destroys, conflict and division (with suffering) caused by the gospel, or the new spiritual life and Spirit Jesus brings. Cambridge takes it in all these senses.

idiom: I have a baptism to undergo
meaning: Jesus speaks of his coming suffering and death as an overwhelming plunge, like being swallowed by deep waters. He feels great inner pressure until it is over.

idiom: that fox
meaning: A contemptuous name for Herod, calling him a sly, cunning, scheming man who works by trickery; the fox stood for craftiness and sneaky attack.

idiom: your house is left to you desolate
meaning: Your house (the temple and city) is abandoned by God and left to you alone; his presence has gone and ruin will soon follow.

idiom: carry his cross
meaning: To accept willingly whatever suffering following Jesus brings, including denying oneself, shame, persecution, and even death.

idiom: Abraham's side
meaning: The happy state of the righteous after death. At meals people reclined with their head near the chest of the person beside them, so lying next to Abraham meant being an honored guest close to him at the heavenly banquet.

idiom: Remember Lot's wife!
meaning: A warning not to delay or look back with longing at a world that is about to be judged, but to flee at once. Lot's wife looked back and was destroyed.

idiom: sons of the resurrection
meaning: People who share in the resurrection to everlasting life; being raised in this way shows they are God's children and will never die again.

idiom: Sit at My right hand
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.

idiom: a footstool for Your feet
meaning: Enemies fully defeated and put under the ruler's feet, under his complete control.

idiom: lift up your heads
meaning: Take heart and look up with hopeful expectation instead of hanging the head in dejection, because deliverance is near.

idiom: sift all of you like wheat
meaning: Satan wants to shake and test the disciples hard with temptation and trouble, the way grain is tossed in a sieve, hoping to show their faith is worthless chaff.

idiom: seated at the right hand of the power of God
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.

idiom: if men do these things while the tree is green, what will happen when it is dry?
meaning: This is a proverb arguing from lesser to greater. A green tree does not burn easily, but a dry one does. If such suffering falls on the innocent one, far worse will come on the guilty, which several sources link to the coming Roman judgment on the nation.

idiom: born not of blood
meaning: Becoming God's child does not come from natural birth or human ancestry, such as being descended from Abraham. It comes from a spiritual birth that God Himself gives.

idiom: My hour has not yet come
meaning: The right moment for Jesus to act had not yet arrived. That moment was set by God, not by others, and in it he would show his power as Messiah. He signals that he will act, but at his own time.

idiom: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again
meaning: A riddle-like prediction. "Temple" means Jesus' own body: when they kill him, he will rise from the dead on the third day, and that will be the sign of his authority.

idiom: The friend of the bridegroom
meaning: The groom's closest friend, who arranged the marriage and ran the wedding feast. He shared fully in the groom's happiness. John the Baptist used it of himself: he had prepared the people for the Messiah and was glad to step back once the people went to Him.

idiom: living water
meaning: In everyday speech it meant flowing spring water, not still water. Jesus used it for the life-giving grace and Spirit He gives, which truly satisfies the soul.

idiom: placed His seal of approval
meaning: God the Father authenticated and endorsed Jesus as the one He sent to give lasting life, the way a seal confirms a document; He did this through miracles, Scripture and the voice from heaven.

idiom: eat the flesh and drink the blood of the Son of Man
meaning: Not literal. It means taking Christ himself, and especially his sacrificial death, into your inner life through faith, as the one source of spiritual life. Mentioning blood separately from flesh points to his violent death, and the words would have shocked Jews, who were forbidden to eat blood.

idiom: your time is always at hand
meaning: Any time suits you; nothing depends on when you act or show yourselves, since the world is not set against you and you are in no danger, unlike Jesus.

idiom: His hour had not yet come
meaning: The time God had set for Jesus' suffering and death (his departure to the Father) had arrived. Before that moment his enemies could only plot against him and could not touch him.

idiom: Streams of living water will flow from within him
meaning: In everyday speech it meant flowing spring water, not still water. Jesus used it for the life-giving grace and Spirit He gives, which truly satisfies the soul.

idiom: see My day
meaning: To witness the time of the Messiah's coming and work. Abraham longed for that time and rejoiced when he saw it, though the sources differ on how he saw it: by faith in God's promises, from the world of the dead after his death, or in his meetings with the Angel of the LORD.

idiom: Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep
meaning: To have died. Sleep is the usual gentle picture for death, especially a believer's death.

idiom: the prince of this world
meaning: Satan, as the ruler of the world that stands against God. Jewish teachers commonly used this title for Satan, whom they saw as lord of the Gentiles. Jesus says his death will overthrow him.

idiom: His hour had come
meaning: The time God had set for Jesus' suffering and death (his departure to the Father) had arrived. Before that moment his enemies could only plot against him and could not touch him.

idiom: has lifted up his heel against Me
meaning: Like a horse that kicks the master who feeds it, or a wrestler who trips someone up. It means a trusted friend who shared his table turned on him in brutal betrayal.

idiom: you will not fall away
meaning: Jesus warned them ahead of time so that persecution would not catch them off guard and trip them into giving up their faith and their work.

idiom: the son of destruction
meaning: A Hebrew way of describing someone by his defining trait: a man marked by ruin and headed for it. Here it means Judas, the one disciple who was lost.

idiom: Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?
meaning: To suffer the share of God's anger and punishment that is assigned to someone, pictured as a cup they are made to drink. In Jeremiah 49:12 the point is that if even God's own people were made to suffer it, Edom has no hope of escaping.

idiom: went in and out among us
meaning: Jesus lived and carried out his ministry among them as their constant companion.

idiom: He is at my right hand
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.

idiom: nor did His body see decay
meaning: To die and rot in the grave. To "not see decay" means to escape death and the grave.

idiom: to the right hand of God
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.

idiom: all who are far off
meaning: People far from God's people: mainly the Gentiles, and possibly also Jews scattered in other lands or later generations.

idiom: to break bread from house to house
meaning: To share the Lord's Supper (communion), held by early Christians when they met on the first day of the week, possibly together with a shared meal.

idiom: completely cut off from among his people
meaning: In this verse, to be destroyed or wiped out, as all living things were killed by the flood.

idiom: hanging Him on a tree
meaning: Putting Jesus to death by crucifixion; "tree" stands for the cross.

idiom: exalted Him to His right hand
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.

idiom: You stiff-necked people with uncircumcised hearts and ears
meaning: Stubborn and rebellious. The picture is a work animal that stiffens its neck and refuses to be steered by its driver or to accept the yoke.

idiom: they gnashed their teeth at him
meaning: Grinding the teeth is a sign of fierce anger and hostility, like a wild beast about to tear its prey. In Job 16:9 it pictures the attacker raging against the sufferer.

idiom: at the right hand of God
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.

idiom: he fell asleep
meaning: To have died. Sleep is the usual gentle picture for death, especially a believer's death.

idiom: The hand of the Lord was with them
meaning: God's power and favor were at work alongside the preachers, making their message take hold so that many came to believe.

idiom: Peter came to himself
meaning: Peter got over his shock and confusion and could think clearly again. He realized his escape had really happened and was not a dream or vision.

idiom: You are out of your mind
meaning: "You're crazy!": a reaction to news that seemed too good to be true, since they thought what she said was impossible.

idiom: the hand of the Lord is against you
meaning: God Himself was punishing the man directly; here He struck him blind, as a correction meant to last only for a time.

idiom: a man after My own heart
meaning: A man God chose who fits what God wants, someone who would carry out God's will (David, in contrast to Saul).

idiom: took Him down from the tree
meaning: They took Jesus' body down from the cross ("tree" being a word for the cross) after His death.

idiom: never to see decay
meaning: To die and rot in the grave. To "not see decay" means to escape death and the grave.

idiom: saw decay
meaning: To die and rot in the grave. To "not see decay" means to escape death and the grave.

idiom: did not see decay
meaning: To die and rot in the grave. To "not see decay" means to escape death and the grave.

idiom: they shook the dust off their feet
meaning: A public sign of breaking off from a place that rejected God's messengers; Jews shook off the dust of pagan lands as unclean, so doing this to a Jewish town treated it as no better than heathen, cut all ties, and left it responsible for its own guilt.

idiom: they tore their clothes
meaning: Ripping one's garments was the strongest sign of horror and grief, used especially in response to blasphemy; here it showed the apostles utterly rejected being worshiped as gods.

idiom: placing on the necks of the disciples a yoke
meaning: Loading believers with a heavy, enslaving obligation, here the duty of keeping the Mosaic law and its rituals. A yoke stood for bondage and burden, and Jews commonly called the law a yoke.

idiom: risked their lives
meaning: They exposed themselves to deadly danger, as in the persecution and stoning on their journeys, for the cause of Christ.

idiom: he shook out his garments
meaning: A symbolic act of breaking off with them and refusing responsibility for them: nothing of theirs would cling to him, and their guilt was their own.

idiom: Your blood be on your own heads!
meaning: The guilt and responsibility for a person's death rests on that person (or on whoever is named), not on anyone else. Someone who dies through his own neglect or choice has only himself to blame.

idiom: to break bread
meaning: To share the Lord's Supper (communion), held by early Christians when they met on the first day of the week, possibly together with a shared meal.

idiom: I am innocent of the blood of all men
meaning: Paul is not to blame if anyone is lost, because he faithfully warned and taught them all, like the watchman in Ezekiel who has done his duty.

idiom: you whitewashed wall!
meaning: You hypocrite: like a wall coated with whitewash, you look fair and righteous on the outside but are not what you seem underneath.

idiom: It is hard for you to kick against the goads
meaning: Taken from an ox that kicks back at the driver's pointed stick and only hurts itself more; resisting God, who is far stronger, is useless and self-harming, so it is better to give in.

idiom: according to the flesh
meaning: As far as his human nature and human ancestry go, in contrast to his divine nature as Son of God.

idiom: have a harvest among you
meaning: To see good results from his ministry among them, with people won to Christ and believers built up, as had happened with other Gentiles.

idiom: walk according to the flesh
meaning: To live and direct one's conduct by the rule and impulses of fallen, sin-dominated human nature, instead of being led by God's Spirit; "walking" stands for the whole direction of one's life.

idiom: put to death the deeds of the body
meaning: To kill off sinful desires and habits completely. That means refusing to feed or tolerate them, so that they lose all their power.

idiom: How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news
meaning: Messengers who bring news of deliverance and salvation are a welcome, delightful sight, like a runner seen coming over the hills with good news. They are loved because of the message they carry.

idiom: To his own master he stands or falls
meaning: A servant answers only to his own master, who alone approves or condemns him; so a believer is accountable to the Lord, not to fellow believers who judge him.

idiom: the Day will bring it to light
meaning: The coming Day of the Lord's judgment will show the true worth of each person's work, testing it like fire. Some sources instead think of a coming time of trial or the passing of time, but the point is the same: what the work really is will be exposed.

idiom: as if through the flames
meaning: Saved only narrowly and with difficulty, losing the work he built, like someone who barely escapes a fire while everything he had is burned up.

idiom: Get rid of the old leaven
meaning: Remove the old sin and corruption, including the offender and the attitude that put up with him, from the church, as Jews searched out every crumb of leaven before Passover. That way the community would really be as pure as its calling says.

idiom: drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons
meaning: Drinking at the Lord's Supper means fellowship with Christ, and drinking the wine offered at idol feasts means fellowship with the demons behind the idols. A believer cannot rightly share in both.

idiom: have fallen asleep
meaning: To have died. Sleep is the usual gentle picture for death, especially a believer's death.

idiom: out of your minds
meaning: Outsiders hearing nothing but uninterpreted tongues would think the congregation were raving fanatics or insane.

idiom: fallen asleep in Christ
meaning: To have died. Sleep is the usual gentle picture for death, especially a believer's death.

idiom: those who have fallen asleep
meaning: To have died. Sleep is the usual gentle picture for death, especially a believer's death.

idiom: fought wild beasts in Ephesus
meaning: Most take it as a figure: Paul faced deadly danger at Ephesus from savage, beast-like opponents, since a Roman citizen could not legally be thrown to animals. Gill argues for a literal fight in the arena, or a supposed case.

idiom: We will not all sleep
meaning: To have died. Sleep is the usual gentle picture for death, especially a believer's death.

idiom: Yes, yes" and also "No, no
meaning: Being unreliable: saying yes and no about the same thing, changing plans on a whim like worldly people do. Some take it the other way, as stubbornly forcing one's yes to stay yes no matter what, and one source calls the clause's exact sense uncertain.

idiom: placed His seal on us
meaning: God has marked believers as His own and confirmed that they are genuine. A seal stamped on a document or property showed ownership, made it official, and kept it secure. God's seal is the gift of His Spirit, which assures believers that they belong to Him.

idiom: leads us triumphantly as captives in Christ
meaning: Based on a Roman victory parade, where a conquering general led captives through incense-filled streets. Some read it as God leading Paul as a conquered captive displayed in Christ's triumph; others read it as God making Paul and his fellow workers share in the victory.

idiom: with unveiled faces
meaning: Unlike Moses, who veiled his face, and unlike those with a veil over their hearts, believers see the Lord's glory openly and clearly, with nothing in between.

idiom: the earthly tent we live in
meaning: The mortal body is a temporary dwelling for the soul, like a tent that is easily taken down. At death it is dismantled, and God provides a permanent home.

idiom: out of our mind
meaning: Critics called Paul mad for his intense zeal, ecstasies and bold claims; he answers that whatever looks like madness is done for God.

idiom: the weapons of righteousness in the right hand and in the left
meaning: Being fully armed on every side, with attacking weapons in one hand and defensive ones in the other; for Paul the armor is a righteous, holy life.

idiom: unequally yoked
meaning: Being bound in a close partnership with unbelievers, as mismatched as an ox and a donkey hitched to the same plow, which the Mosaic law forbade. It includes marriage but also extends to other intimate ties, such as joining in idol worship, because believers and unbelievers have no common ground.

idiom: out of my mind
meaning: Paul admits that boasting about himself is like talking as a madman, perhaps throwing his critics' insult back at them, but he is forced into it to answer his rivals.

idiom: the right hand of fellowship
meaning: Clasping right hands was a sign of friendship and agreement; by it the Jerusalem leaders publicly recognized Paul and Barnabas as true partners and colleagues in the work, sealing a pledge to the same gospel with separate mission fields.

idiom: you have fallen away from grace
meaning: Anyone who tries to be made right with God by keeping the law gives up the way of God's free favor through Christ, and so loses their place in it.

idiom: seated Him at His right hand
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.

idiom: redeeming the time
meaning: To make the most of every opportunity. Like a merchant buying up a valuable item, you seize each chance to do good and use it well, because an evil age is full of distractions and temptations.

idiom: your feet fitted with the readiness of the gospel of peace
meaning: Like a soldier's sturdy sandals, the gospel of peace gives the believer what he needs on his feet; some take this as readiness to march or act, others as firm footing that lets him stand steady and unafraid.

idiom: poured out like a drink offering
meaning: Giving up one's life, here Paul's possible death as a martyr, as an offering to God. It alludes to the wine poured over or beside a sacrifice. Paul pictures his blood as that libation, added to the sacrifice of his converts' faith.

idiom: Watch out for those dogs
meaning: "Dog" was an insult for someone unclean, shameless, snarling, and outcast. Jews used it for Gentiles. Paul turns it back on the Judaizing teachers, saying they are the true outsiders and troublemakers.

idiom: my true yokefellow
meaning: A faithful partner who shares the same work as Paul, like an ox pulling under the same yoke; who is meant is unknown (perhaps Epaphroditus or a leader at Philippi), and some think it is a personal name, Syzygus.

idiom: the fruit that may be credited to your account
meaning: Using the language of bookkeeping and interest, Paul says that what he wants is not their gift but the reward that grows from it and is recorded in their favor before God.

idiom: seated at the right hand of God
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.

idiom: Put to death
meaning: To kill off sinful desires and habits completely. That means refusing to feed or tolerate them, so that they lose all their power.

idiom: seasoned with salt
meaning: Speech that is wholesome, pleasant, and to the point. Salt both preserves food and gives it flavor, so this speech is neither corrupt nor dull, and it fits each person who asks a question.

idiom: our crown of boasting
meaning: The people Paul is proudest of, like the victory wreath an athlete wore after winning in the games; his converts will be his joy and honor when Christ returns.

idiom: those who have fallen asleep in Him
meaning: To have died. Sleep is the usual gentle picture for death, especially a believer's death.

idiom: let us not sleep as the others do, but let us remain awake and sober
meaning: Believers must not slide into the spiritual carelessness of unbelievers. They should stay alert and ready for the Lord's coming, and live with self-control instead of indulgence.

idiom: taken out of the way
meaning: To be removed or withdrawn. Once the restraining power is gone, the lawlessness that now works in secret will appear openly. Who the restrainer is remains disputed, but not what the phrase means.

idiom: the breath of His mouth
meaning: The Lord overthrows his enemy with nothing more than what comes from his mouth (his breath or word), which shows his overwhelming power and how little effort it costs him. Some take it as the spoken gospel working over time, others as his power at his return, but either way his word alone is enough.

idiom: handed over to Satan
meaning: Putting offenders out of the church and into Satan's realm, often understood as bringing bodily suffering on them, as a punishment meant to correct them and stop their blasphemy. Sources differ on whether the main point is expulsion, physical affliction, or both.

idiom: in season and out of season
meaning: It means at all times. The preacher should keep at the work urgently and seize every chance, whether the time suits him and his hearers or not, and even in danger or discouragement.

idiom: with itching ears
meaning: Hungry to hear something pleasing or new. Like an itch that wants scratching, these listeners crave teaching that flatters them and leaves their desires alone, and they collect teachers who will give them that.

idiom: being poured out like a drink offering
meaning: Giving up one's life, here Paul's possible death as a martyr, as an offering to God. It alludes to the wine poured over or beside a sacrifice. Paul pictures his blood as that libation, added to the sacrifice of his converts' faith.

idiom: refreshed the hearts of the saints
meaning: Philemon's love and generous help gave believers' inner feelings rest and relief from their troubles and burdens, cheering them deeply.

idiom: Refresh my heart in Christ
meaning: Ease my deep, anxious feelings and make me glad by granting this request, as an act of love in Christ.

idiom: at the right hand of the Majesty on high
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.

idiom: Their hearts are always going astray
meaning: The people were inclined by nature to wander from God in their will and affections, and they kept on doing it; forty years of rebellion showed what their character was.

idiom: laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works
meaning: A building image: the basic first teachings, such as turning away from lifeless works done without spiritual life, are the foundation. They are already laid and should not be laid over and over; believers should build on them toward maturity.

idiom: have fallen away
meaning: A complete, deliberate rejection of Christ and the Christian faith after having known it, going back to unbelief and siding with his enemies.

idiom: in the loin of his ancestor
meaning: Levi was not yet born, but he was counted as already present in his forefather Abraham. So what Abraham did, paying tithes to Melchizedek, was treated as done by his descendants too.

idiom: sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven
meaning: To have someone at your right hand means having them close beside you as a protector, defender, or champion, like a fellow warrior standing on your right. It can also mark a place of honor.

idiom: a footstool for His feet
meaning: Enemies fully defeated and put under the ruler's feet, under his complete control.

idiom: through the curtain of His body
meaning: Christ's body, given in death, is compared to the temple veil the high priest passed through into the Most Holy Place; through His sacrificed flesh the way into God's presence is opened.

idiom: having our hearts sprinkled
meaning: Our inner selves have been cleansed of guilt by Christ's blood, like priests sprinkled with blood before they could approach God.

idiom: you were in the light
meaning: When you were first enlightened, that is, when you came to know the truth and became Christians (linked by some with baptism).

idiom: a great cloud of witnesses
meaning: A huge crowd (in Greek, Latin and Hebrew a "cloud" meant a great number) of earlier faithful people. They prove that faith pays off, and they are pictured all around believers like spectators in the stands at a race, which should push believers to keep going.

idiom: the fruit of lips
meaning: Spoken praise and thanksgiving to God, which the lips "bear" like fruit, offered as a sacrifice in place of the old animal and thank offerings.

idiom: You adulteresses
meaning: Spiritually unfaithful people. Drawing on the Old Testament picture of God as husband to his people, those who love the world have broken faith with God, like a wife cheating on her husband.

idiom: You have fattened your hearts in the day of slaughter
meaning: The rich have indulged themselves to the full like cattle fattened for slaughter, feeding happily even as their day of judgment and ruin arrives. Some read it as living every day like a lavish feast after a sacrifice.

idiom: cover over a multitude of sins
meaning: To bring about the forgiveness of many sins, so they are hidden from God's judgment. Here it mainly means the sins of the person brought back from wrongdoing.

idiom: like sheep going astray
meaning: Before conversion people were like a flock with no shepherd: they had wandered off on their own paths, had no protector, and were in danger until they were brought back to the true Shepherd.

idiom: love covers over a multitude of sins
meaning: Love overlooks, forgives and does not expose the many faults of others, so it keeps the peace instead of stirring up strife.

idiom: this tent will soon be laid aside
meaning: The mortal body is a temporary dwelling for the soul, like a tent that is easily taken down. At death it is dismantled, and God provides a permanent home.

idiom: the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts
meaning: Prophecy is like a lamp in a dark place, to be followed until a fuller light comes. Some take that light to be Christ's return in glory; others take it to be Christ himself made fully known and present inside the believer, like the morning star that comes before the full day.

idiom: their destruction does not sleep
meaning: The ruin decreed for them is not idle or put off. It is awake, watching them, and moving toward them, and it will strike at the appointed time, even if it seems to be delayed.

idiom: our fathers fell asleep
meaning: To have died. Sleep is the usual gentle picture for death, especially a believer's death.

idiom: send them on their way
meaning: To help travelers on their journey by giving them supplies, hospitality, and sometimes an escort, and seeing them off with honor.

idiom: traveled the path of Cain
meaning: They followed Cain's way of life, the first great example of wickedness, marked by envy, hatred of the righteous and defiance of God.

idiom: hidden reefs in your love feasts
meaning: The false teachers at the church's shared fellowship meals are like rocks hidden under the sea: unnoticed dangers that wreck the faith of people who get close to them. The older rendering "spots" reads them instead as stains or blemishes that disgrace the meals.

idiom: twice dead after being uprooted
meaning: Completely and hopelessly dead, like a barren tree pulled out by its roots that can never bear fruit again. Some sources read the "twice" as two deaths: dead in their natural state, then dead again after falling away from the faith they once professed.

idiom: wandering stars
meaning: False teachers who are unstable and unreliable, like heavenly bodies that do not keep a steady course. Sources compare them to planets that seem to wander, or to comets and meteors that blaze briefly and then vanish into darkness. Their fame is short and their influence harmful.

idiom: wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own shame
meaning: The false teachers are as restless, loud and uncontrolled as stormy waves, and like waves throwing up foam and filth, all their noise only shows off their own disgraceful deeds and empty teaching.

idiom: the sword of My mouth
meaning: Christ's spoken word used as a weapon, declaring judgment on the wrongdoers and carrying it out.

idiom: have not soiled their garments
meaning: They kept themselves morally pure and true to their faith, not stained by the corruption around them.

idiom: holds the key of David
meaning: Christ has full royal authority over God's house and kingdom, like the palace steward given the king's key in Isaiah 22:22. He alone decides who gets in and who is shut out, and no one can overrule him.

idiom: neither cold nor hot
meaning: Being lukewarm: claiming faith but having no real zeal, neither burning with devotion nor openly untouched by it, a careless and self-satisfied state that Christ finds worse than either extreme.

idiom: the Root of David
meaning: The Messiah as the shoot that grows from David's family line: David's true descendant and heir, with the right to rule on his throne. Some add that he is also David's source and Lord.

idiom: hide us from the face of the One seated on the throne
meaning: A terrified wish to escape the presence and judgment of God and the Lamb. They would rather die or vanish than face His wrath.

idiom: washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb
meaning: To be cleansed from sin through the blood of Christ, the Lamb. This is what gives people the right to eat from the tree of life and enter the heavenly city.

idiom: throw dust on their heads
meaning: A common sign of grief, mourning and humiliation, showing they had been brought low or shared another's sorrow.

idiom: from His mouth proceeds a sharp sword
meaning: Christ's spoken word, his sentence of judgment, acts as his weapon: by his word alone he strikes down and destroys the nations that oppose him.

idiom: He treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty
meaning: God (seen as the Messiah) has crushed his enemies in judgment single-handedly, with no human help. The winepress stands for the slaughter of battle, and the stains on his clothes are their blood.

idiom: wash their robes
meaning: To be cleansed from sin through the blood of Christ, the Lamb. This is what gives people the right to eat from the tree of life and enter the heavenly city.

idiom: outside are the dogs
meaning: "Dog" was an insult for someone unclean, shameless, snarling, and outcast. Jews used it for Gentiles. Paul turns it back on the Judaizing teachers, saying they are the true outsiders and troublemakers.
